payload.name: Resolve relative dates in extracted content
payload.description: When extracting a memory whose source text uses a relative time expression (e.g., 'next month', 'last week', 'in two days'), resolve it to the absolute date from the message timestamp and write that date in the content string.
content: During extraction, if the source message contains a relative time expression (e.g., 'next month', 'last week', 'tomorrow'), resolve it against the message/session timestamp and write the resulting absolute date in the memory content string, not only in world_start/world_end.
If the timestamp is missing or the reference is genuinely ambiguous, keep the relative phrase but do not invent a specific date; flag the uncertainty instead.

candidates.solves: During extraction, relative time phrases are often kept verbatim in content even when world_start/world_end are resolved, so later date queries fail. This rule makes memory content self-contained by replacing relative expressions with the absolute date from the session timestamp. It applies to future extractions of plans, events, or states with relative time; not to quotes where the phrase must be preserved.

payload.name: Preserve resolved relative times in event memories
payload.description: When a message states an event happened at a relative time (last week, yesterday, a few days ago), resolve it against the message/session timestamp and include the resolved time in extraction candidates and memory content.
content: During candidate extraction, if a message describes an event with a relative time expression (e.g., 'last week', 'yesterday', 'a few days ago'), resolve it against the message/session timestamp and include the resolved actual date or period in the candidate's content and world_start.

When creating or updating event memories, keep the specific timing of an action distinct from the report date: if the message date is 14 August and the event occurred 'last week', record the event as occurring in early August rather than on the message date.
Do not drop temporal detail just because it is relative; preserve the resolved time so future questions about when the event occurred remain answerable.

candidates.solves: Event extraction can lose relative time phrases (e.g., 'last week') when recording memories, leaving later questions about when the event happened unanswerable. The rule: whenever a source message anchors an event with a relative time, resolve it against the message timestamp and preserve the resolved date/period in content and world_start. Applicable to any future construction where timing is expressed relationally; not needed for messages that already contain an explicit absolute date.

payload.name: Extract past events from conversational user messages
payload.description: When a user mentions a personal past action with a time reference (e.g., 'Last Friday I made...') in a casual or conversational message, extract an event candidate during construction.
content: During extraction, treat every user statement reporting a personal past action as an event candidate, even if the message is informal, uses playful language, or primarily asks a question.
Resolve relative time expressions (e.g., 'last Friday', 'yesterday', 'last week') against the message timestamp to produce an absolute date for the event.
Do not skip extraction because the action topic seems unrelated to the ongoing theme; preserve factual past events regardless of their discourse role.

candidates.solves: The extraction stage missed a clear user-reported past event because the message was conversational and the factual statement was incidental to the main question. Future inputs containing casual, informal user statements about personal past actions with time references should still yield event candidates; the rule applies across topics and is bounded to factual past actions, not hypotheticals or future plans.

payload.name: ResolveRelativeTimesInMemoryContent
payload.description: Use when creating or updating memories from messages that mention time relatively, such as 'last month', 'yesterday', or 'a week ago'.
content: During extraction, resolve relative temporal expressions (e.g., 'last month', 'yesterday', 'X days ago') to absolute dates using the message/session timestamp, and write the resolved date (e.g., 'May 2023') in the memory content instead of the relative phrase.
Apply this in both extraction and CRUD stages: when a candidate or update contains a relative time expression, replace it with the corresponding absolute date before generating content.

candidates.solves: When constructing memories from messages containing relative time expressions (e.g., 'last month', 'yesterday'), extraction may preserve the relative phrase, losing the absolute date even when world_start is computed. This skill requires resolving relative time to an absolute date from the message/session timestamp and embedding the precise date in memory content so future recall is unambiguous.

payload.name: ResolveRelativeTimeInExtraction
payload.description: When constructing a memory from a message containing a relative time expression and a message/session timestamp is available, resolve it to an absolute date during extraction.
content: During candidate extraction, if a message contains a relative time expression (e.g., 'yesterday', 'last week', 'last month', 'last year', 'two days ago'), resolve it to an absolute date using the message/session timestamp before forming the candidate.
Write the resolved absolute date in the memory content and in structured time fields such as world_start/world_end; do not substitute vague words like 'recently'.
If the timestamp is missing or the relative expression cannot be resolved, keep the original phrase and do not invent a specific date.

candidates.solves: Extraction failed when a relative time phrase such as 'last month' was stored as 'recently', losing the absolute date needed later. Resolve relative time expressions (yesterday, last week/month/year, two days ago) to absolute dates using the message/session timestamp during candidate extraction. This applies to future event-memory construction whenever such phrases appear and a timestamp exists; it does not apply when the timestamp is missing or the expression is intentionally vague.

payload.name: ExtractVagueEventWithRelativeTime
payload.description: When a message states the speaker attended or went to an event, even if described vaguely or informally, and includes a relative time phrase like 'last week' or 'yesterday', extract an event memory and resolve the absolute date from the message timestamp.
content: During extraction, if a speaker states they attended, went to, or participated in an event, create an event memory candidate even when the event is described vaguely (e.g., 'a cool event', 'a meetup') or lacks a proper name.

When the message uses a relative time phrase ('last week', 'yesterday', 'a few days ago'), resolve it to an absolute date using the message or session timestamp and store that resolved date in the memory's occurred_at.

candidates.solves: The Construction Agent generated no extraction candidate for a message where the user mentioned attending 'a cool event last week' because the phrasing was informal and the event name was absent. This abstract rule covers any future message that reports event participation with a relative time phrase (e.g., 'went to a meetup', 'saw a show', 'attended a gathering') and requires extracting an event memory with the date resolved from the message/session timestamp. It does not apply when no event participation is stated or when the date is already explicit.

payload.name: Resolve relative time to absolute dates in memories
payload.description: When creating or updating event/plan memories from messages that contain relative time expressions (last Sunday, yesterday, ago), resolve them to absolute dates using the message timestamp before writing content or world_start.
content: When constructing memory candidates or updating existing memories, resolve any relative time references (e.g., 'last Sunday', 'yesterday', 'three days ago') to absolute calendar dates using the message's occurred_at timestamp.
Set world_start (and world_end if resolvable) to the absolute date; do not use the message date or a guessed nearby date as a substitute.
Store the resolved absolute date explicitly in content (e.g., 'on 2023-06-11') instead of preserving relative phrasing, so the memory remains self-contained and retrievable by date queries.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause was that extraction preserved a relative time phrase ('previous Sunday') and an incorrect world_start instead of converting it to the absolute date implied by the message timestamp, so the memory lacked an explicit date and could only partially support retrieval. The abstraction is a general rule: whenever a message states an event or plan relative to its sending time, memory construction must resolve that reference to an absolute calendar date. This applies to any future event/plan extraction or update across all topics.

payload.name: Resolve relative event dates before storing event memories
payload.description: When extracting an event whose time is relative to the message (yesterday, today, last week, etc.), compute its actual date from the message timestamp before setting world_start.
content: During extraction, if an event's time is relative (yesterday, today, tomorrow, last week), resolve it using the message/session timestamp and store the resulting actual date as world_start.
Do not use the message occurrence date as the event date unless the message explicitly says the event occurred then.

candidates.solves: Extraction can record the message date as the event date when an event is described with a relative time expression such as 'yesterday' or 'last week'. The rule requires resolving relative expressions against the message/session timestamp to obtain the actual event date before setting world_start. It applies to event extraction in conversational memory construction, but not to messages that state an explicit date.

payload.name: ResolveRelativeTimeForEventDates
payload.description: When an event's time is stated with a relative expression (last week, yesterday, recently), compute the event date from the message timestamp instead of using the message date.
content: During extraction or CRUD of an event memory, when the source message states the event time using a relative expression (e.g., 'last week', 'yesterday', 'two days ago', 'recently'), resolve the event's start date by applying that offset to the message's occurred_at timestamp; do not set the event date to the message's occurred_at date itself unless the expression is 'today' or 'now'.

If the relative expression is ambiguous (e.g., 'recently'), prefer the most recent plausible date consistent with the conversation and message timestamp, and do not overwrite a more specific existing event memory without supporting evidence.

candidates.solves: Extraction misresolved the relative expression 'last week' as the message date, writing an inaccurate event date. The abstract mechanism is treating relative temporal expressions as absolute dates when constructing event memories. This rule—resolve relative expressions by applying the offset to the message's occurred_at timestamp—applies to any future message using 'yesterday', 'last week', 'recently', etc., and prevents the same date error across topics.

payload.name: Extract purchase events from relative-clause modifiers
payload.description: When a noun phrase is modified by a relative clause expressing a purchase, acquisition, or other dated event (e.g., 'that I bought'), extract that event as its own memory for the modified object, with the relative time resolved against the message timestamp.
content: During extraction, when a message contains an object noun with a relative clause denoting a purchase/acquisition and a relative time expression (e.g., 'the X that I bought the day before yesterday'), create a separate event candidate: subject=buyer, content names the purchased object explicitly, and world_start = resolved purchase date.

When checking existing memories, do not SKIP such a candidate merely because the buyer or noun already appears in memory; verify whether the specific purchase event for that object is already stored, and if not, propose ADD.
Resolve relative time phrases ('yesterday', 'day before yesterday', 'last week') from the message/session timestamp so the stored event carries an absolute date.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is mis-parsing a relative-clause purchase modifier ('the X that I bought ...') into the subject's existing memory, dropping the real purchase event. The rule—extract such relative-clause events as separate dated memories and verify coverage before skipping—applies to any future message where an object is described by a purchase/acquisition relative clause with a relative time expression.

payload.name: Resolve relative event occurrence dates
payload.description: When a message states an event time using a relative expression (e.g., 'on Friday', 'yesterday', 'last week', 'next Monday'), resolve it against the message/session timestamp and store the absolute date as the event's occurrence date.
content: When an event memory is created or updated from a message stating the event time relative to the message date (e.g., 'on Friday', 'yesterday', 'last week'), resolve it against the message/session timestamp and set the event world_start to that absolute occurrence date.

Preserve the occurrence date in the memory even if a later future or plan date is also mentioned; use the occurrence date as the event's world_start or add a separate event for the plan date rather than dropping the occurrence date.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: an event memory omitted its occurrence date when the message reported it relative to the message date (e.g., 'on Friday'), and a later plan date was used as world_start instead. The reusable rule is to resolve relative time against the message timestamp and store the absolute event date. Applies to any event construction where relative time is resolvable; not applicable when the relative expression cannot be resolved to a specific date.

payload.name: Resolve relative durations to absolute dates
payload.description: When a message states a duration relative to the present (e.g., 'for N years', 'N years ago') describing how long something has been true, compute the absolute start date from the message timestamp and store it.
content: During extraction, when a message says how long something has been true (e.g., 'I've had X for N years', 'we've lived here N months'), compute the absolute start date by subtracting the duration from the message/session timestamp and set it as the event's start time, not the message date.
Store the resolved absolute date as the primary fact and do not replicate only the relative phrase, so future 'when did X begin?' questions remain answerable.
During CRUD, if an existing memory contains only a relative duration, update it to include the resolved absolute start date derived from the original message timestamp.

candidates.solves: Relative duration phrases (e.g., 'for three years') were stored verbatim without the implied absolute start date, leaving later questions about when an event began unanswered. This rule back-computes the absolute start date from the message timestamp and stores it, applying to any session where a message states how long something has been true (possessions, jobs, residences, relationships).

payload.name: Resolve relative time to event date
payload.description: When extracting or updating an event memory from a message that uses relative time words like yesterday, today, or last week, resolve them against the message/session timestamp.
content: During extraction: if the source message describes an event with a relative time expression (e.g., yesterday, today, this week), resolve it to the absolute date using the message/session timestamp (yesterday = timestamp date minus one day) and set world_start to that resolved event date; do not set world_start to the message timestamp or an existing memory date.

During CRUD/update: when updating or enriching an existing event memory with a newly dated event from the message, set world_start to the newly resolved event date instead of retaining an older world_start from the previous version.
Include the resolved absolute date in the event memory content when the event date is part of the stated fact.

candidates.solves: Messages describing an event with relative time words (yesterday, today, last week) must resolve the date from the message timestamp and store it as world_start, replacing any older world_start during updates. This prevents the message timestamp or a stale memory date from masking the true event date. Applies to future event extraction from relative-time statements; not to messages with explicit absolute dates.

payload.name: Resolve relative time to world_start in events
payload.description: When constructing or updating event memories from messages that use relative time phrases (e.g., 'last Friday', 'yesterday'), resolve them to concrete dates and preserve the resolved date as world_start.
content: When extracting an event, if the evidence states a relative time expression (e.g., 'last Friday', 'yesterday', 'a few days ago'), resolve it against the message/session timestamp to compute the concrete world_start date; never default world_start to the message timestamp itself.

During enrichment or updates of an existing event memory, keep the originally resolved world_start unless the new message explicitly restates or revises the event date; do not overwrite it with the timestamp of a later message about a different aspect of the same topic.

candidates.solves: Event memories lose their date anchor when relative time phrases ('last Friday') are dropped or mapped to the message timestamp, and when later updates overwrite world_start without new date evidence. This rule resolves relative references to concrete dates during extraction and keeps world_start stable during enrichment unless new evidence revises the date. Applies to any future event-recording session using relative time references.

payload.name: Resolve implicit dates in plan extractions
payload.description: When a user message states a plan or commitment using a relative time expression (e.g., tomorrow, next week, tonight), generate an extraction candidate and resolve the date from the message timestamp.
content: During extraction, treat explicit and implicit date references equally: if a message expresses a plan, arrangement, or commitment with a relative time expression (e.g., 'tomorrow', 'next week', 'tonight'), create a candidate for an 'event' or 'plan' memory.
Resolve relative time expressions using the message/session timestamp as the anchor; record the absolute date in the memory rather than the relative phrase.
Do not skip a message as non-extractable solely because the date is implicit; verify whether a plan or commitment is present.

candidates.solves: The extraction stage failed to generate any candidate for a message that contained a future plan expressed only through a relative date ('tomorrow' from 9 November 2022), leaving memory empty. The reusable mechanism is that plans with implicit dates are undervalued during candidate extraction. This Skill applies to any construction session where a user message states a plan or commitment with a relative time reference; it does not apply to messages without plans or to explicit-date statements that are already handled.

payload.name: Extract concrete events with relative time references
payload.description: During extraction, when a message contains a specific event with a relative time expression alongside general commentary, extract the event separately and resolve its time to an absolute date.
content: When a message mixes general commentary with a specific event, create a distinct candidate for the event instead of folding it into a topical summary.
Resolve relative time expressions (e.g., 'last year', 'this summer') using the message or session timestamp to obtain an absolute year/date.
Use memory_kind 'event' for that event, putting the resolved time in world_start.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates often capture only the conversational topic while dropping a concrete fact embedded in the same message, such as a past trip with a relative time expression. This leaves no memory to answer later factual queries. The rule applies when one message mixes general commentary with a specific event and a relative time reference; extraction should create a separate event memory and resolve the relative time against the message/session timestamp.

payload.name: Resolve-weekday-event-dates
payload.description: When extracting an event memory whose time is given as a weekday name (e.g., 'on Friday', 'last Tuesday') in a message with a known occurred_at timestamp, resolve the weekday to the concrete date and store it as world_start.
content: During extraction, when a message with a known occurred_at timestamp describes an event using a bare weekday name ('on Friday', 'last Tuesday'), resolve it to the most recent occurrence of that weekday before the message date (or on that date if context indicates same-day) and set the event's world_start to that resolved date.
Write the resolved date explicitly into the event content (e.g., 'Friday 10 March 2023') instead of only repeating the weekday name, so the temporal relationship is preserved.
Do not default world_start to the message date when the source clearly describes an earlier event; always check relative-time expressions against the message timestamp.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: the extraction candidate set world_start to the message date even though the source described a past event with a weekday reference ('on Friday'), losing the true date (the Friday before the message). The rule resolves bare weekday references against the message/session timestamp to a concrete date, preserving accurate temporal anchors in event memories. Applies whenever a message with a known timestamp describes an event with an unqualified weekday or relative-day expression; does not apply to explicit absolute dates or future plans with explicit dates.

payload.name: ExtractEventClaimsWithRelativeTime
payload.description: When a message contains an explicit statement about a past event or activity with a relative time phrase (e.g., 'last summer', 'last year', 'recently'), extract an event or state memory candidate and resolve the date from the message timestamp.
content: During extraction, treat explicit statements about past events or activities as event/state memory candidates even when they appear in casual or descriptive messages (e.g., sharing photos, storytelling).
If the claim contains a relative time expression ('last summer', 'last year', 'a few months ago'), resolve the absolute date using the message's timestamp before creating the candidate.
Do not skip a claim because it is not the main topic of the message; any explicit factual claim about the user is extractable.

candidates.solves: The construction pipeline missed an explicit claim because it was embedded in a casual photo-sharing message and used a relative time phrase ('last summer'). The abstract failure is that explicit user statements about past events with relative time expressions are not consistently extracted. The rule applies to any future message where the user states a past event or activity with a relative time reference, requiring extraction of an event or state memory with the absolute time resolved from the message timestamp.

payload.name: Extract self-reported past events with resolved relative time
payload.description: When a message contains a speaker's own past action described with a relative time expression (e.g., 'last week', 'yesterday'), create an event candidate for that speaker during extraction and resolve the time to absolute dates from the message timestamp.
content: During extraction, when a speaker describes their own past activity or action using a relative time phrase (e.g., 'last week', 'yesterday', 'a few days ago'), always create an event memory candidate with the speaker as subject, even if the message also contains other salient topics about other people.

Resolve relative time expressions to absolute dates using the message's occurred_at timestamp: e.g., 'last week' maps to the seven-day period immediately before the message date, 'yesterday' to the day before. Set world_start to the resolved date (or start of the resolved range) when creating the candidate.

Do not fold the speaker's self-reported event into another person's memory simply because the same message discusses other activities; keep the speaker's own event as its own compact, evidence-bound candidate.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction can omit a speaker's own past action when the message also contains other salient topics, especially when the action is introduced with a relative time phrase such as 'last week' or 'yesterday'. This rule ensures durable event candidates are created for the speaker's self-reported past activities and that relative time references are resolved to absolute dates using the message's occurred_at timestamp. It applies to any future conversation where a participant describes their own recent actions.

payload.name: ResolveRelativeTimeInExtraction
payload.description: When extracting a fact from a message that states an event time using relative expressions (yesterday, today, tomorrow, last week, X days ago), resolve it to an absolute date from the message/session timestamp before creating a memory candidate.
content: During extraction, if a speaker references an event time using a relative expression (e.g., yesterday, today, tomorrow, last night, this morning, X days/weeks/months ago), resolve the absolute date using the message's occurred_at timestamp and create an explicit event memory with that resolved date.
Do not skip extraction solely because the date is not stated absolutely; if the relative reference is unambiguous, extract the fact with the resolved date.
If the occurred_at timestamp is missing or the relative expression is ambiguous (e.g., 'a while ago'), do not fabricate a date; instead create no memory for that time-bound claim.

candidates.solves: Extraction failures occur when a user states an event with a relative date (e.g., 'yesterday', 'today', 'last week') and the construction agent creates no memory because the absolute date is not explicitly written. This rule applies generally to any conversation where messages carry timestamps and speakers reference events relative to the moment of speaking. It is not for vague references like 'sometime ago' or for cases where the timestamp is missing, because those require inference beyond safe extraction.

payload.name: Resolve relative temporal phrases into absolute dates
payload.description: When extracting a plan or event containing relative time words like 'next month', 'tomorrow', 'this weekend', or 'in two weeks', resolve them against the message/session timestamp before storing the memory.
content: During extraction, convert relative time references (e.g., 'next month', 'tomorrow', 'next week') into the absolute month/date using the timestamp of the message or session.
Store the resolved absolute period in the memory content (and world_start/world_end when applicable) instead of preserving the relative phrase.
If the reference date cannot be determined from available timestamps, note the uncertainty but do not guess a specific date.

candidates.solves: This addresses construction failures where a relative temporal phrase in evidence is stored literally, so later retrieval cannot answer questions about the actual timing. The rule applies to any future plan/event extraction that contains relative time expressions and has a message/session timestamp to resolve them.

payload.name: ResolveRelativeTimeFromMessageTimestamp
payload.description: When extracting or updating an event memory and a message contains a relative time phrase like 'last Sunday', 'yesterday', or 'last week', anchor the date using the message/session timestamp.
content: During candidate extraction, when a message contains a relative time phrase (e.g., 'last Sunday', 'yesterday', 'last week', 'two days ago'), resolve world_start from the message/session occurred_at timestamp: for 'last X' use the most recent X before that timestamp, for 'yesterday' use the day before, and so on.
Do not assign a fixed calendar date to a bare weekday that has no relative modifier (e.g., 'on Sunday') when the intended week is ambiguous; preserve the ambiguity instead of guessing a future date.

During UPDATE/MERGE or enrichment, do not overwrite an already-resolved event world_start with a later date taken from unrelated current-topic context unless a new message confirms the same event occurred again.

candidates.solves: Extraction or update of event memories frequently loses relative temporal references such as 'last Sunday', 'yesterday', or 'last week', producing a wrong or missing world_start that later fails time-based queries. In this diagnosis the phrase 'last Sunday' was reduced to a bare weekday and anchored after the message date. This Skill applies whenever a message timestamp is available to anchor such relative expressions; it does not apply to absolute dates or to messages without a usable timestamp anchor.

payload.name: Resolve-relative-time-in-event-extraction
payload.description: When extracting an event memory whose source message uses a relative time phrase (e.g., 'last week', 'last month'), resolve it to an absolute start date from the message timestamp before setting world_start.
content: During extraction, if an event memory candidate's source message uses a relative time phrase (e.g., 'last week', 'last month', 'yesterday', 'a few days ago'), resolve it to an absolute date using the message/session timestamp. Set world_start to the start of the referenced period: for 'last week' use the start of the previous calendar week (which may be in the previous month); for 'last month' use the first day of the previous month. Never default to the message date, the current date, or the first day of the message's month.

Record the resolved absolute date as world_start and replace the bare relative phrase in the memory content with the resolved absolute period so the memory remains interpretable without the message timestamp.

candidates.solves: Extraction of event memories sometimes copies relative time phrases like 'last week' into content and resolves world_start to the message date or the first day of the message's month, losing the true referenced period which may lie in a previous month. This rule forces resolution of relative time from the message timestamp to the start of the referenced calendar period before storing the memory. It applies whenever an utterance anchors an event with 'last week', 'yesterday', 'last month', or similar, and should not override explicit absolute dates in the text.

payload.name: ResolveRelativeWeekendFromMessageTimestamp
payload.description: When extracting memory from messages that use relative weekend phrases such as 'last weekend', 'this weekend', or 'the weekend before/after', resolve their dates from the message timestamp before recording world_start or world_end.
content: During extraction, anchor any relative weekend phrase ('last weekend', 'this weekend', 'next weekend', 'the weekend before/after X') to the message's own timestamp before setting world_start/world_end.
For 'last weekend', use the most recent Saturday-Sunday block that ends before the message date; do not start on the message date or include following weekdays.
If the message states an exact date or 'the weekend before/after <date>', compute from that date rather than shifting to adjacent weekdays.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: 'last weekend' in an Oct 17 message was misread as Oct 15-16, including Monday, instead of the preceding Sat-Sun Oct 14-15, and the wrong event date was persisted. The reusable mechanism is misanchoring relative calendar phrases during extraction. This rule applies whenever a future message uses a relative weekend phrase and the Construction Agent must set event dates; it does not apply to explicit absolute dates or to non-calendar relative phrases.

payload.name: Relative-date resolution and plural-subject event extraction
payload.description: When extracting events from messages with relative time expressions (e.g., last Friday, yesterday) or first-person plural subjects (we, our), use during extraction to compute exact dates from the message timestamp and preserve all participants.
content: During extraction, resolve relative time expressions (e.g., 'last Friday', 'yesterday', 'this weekend') using the message timestamp to compute the exact calendar date before writing the memory; verify the weekday aligns with the relative expression.

When the speaker describes an activity using first-person plural ('we', 'us', 'our'), extract the event with all implied participants—the speaker and their partner/companion—rather than attributing the activity solely to the speaker. Preserve plural participation in the memory content.

candidates.solves: Concrete problem: extraction misdates relative expressions like 'last Friday' by not anchoring to the message timestamp and drops plural participants from 'we'. This skill applies to future event extractions involving relative time or first-person plural subjects; it does not apply to absolute dates or activities attributed solely to the speaker.

payload.name: Resolve relative times to absolute dates during extraction
payload.description: Use when extracting memories from messages containing relative time phrases (e.g., 'last weekend', 'yesterday', 'this week'); resolve them to absolute calendar dates using the message/session timestamp.
content: When a source message uses a relative time expression (e.g., 'last weekend', 'yesterday', 'this morning'), resolve it to an absolute date using the message's occurred_at timestamp before creating or updating an event/state memory.
Store the resolved absolute date in the memory content and set world_start/world_end to the actual date range; do not preserve the relative phrase as the only temporal anchor.
If the exact date is uncertain, anchor to the best resolved range and avoid ambiguous relative wording in the stored memory.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates sometimes preserve relative temporal phrases like 'last weekend' verbatim, losing the concrete date needed to answer later questions. Resolving such phrases against the source message timestamp creates durable, queryable event memories. This applies to any future construction session where a message references a time relative to its send date.

payload.name: Keep per-speaker preferences separate during extraction
payload.description: When multiple participants express similar personal preferences or admiration in one conversation, apply during extraction: create a separate profile memory for each speaker's own statements; do not merge them into one memory about a single speaker.
content: During extraction, when a message contains a first-person expression of preference, admiration, or opinion (e.g., 'I love...', 'I find... inspiring'), attribute it to the message's speaker alone.

If two or more speakers express similar sentiments in nearby messages, do not combine them into a single candidate about one speaker. Generate one candidate per speaker, each with its own subject and its own stated reasons.
When writing a profile memory, include only reasons or examples that the attributed speaker actually stated; do not import another speaker's rationale into that memory.

candidates.solves: When multiple participants each state their own preference or admiration, extraction may merge them into one speaker's profile and lose others' claims. Apply per-speaker attribution: each first-person statement creates a separate memory for its speaker, even if topics overlap. Future multi-party conversations with similar personal opinions benefit.

payload.name: Extract explicit role-suitability opinions
payload.description: When a message explicitly states that one person's qualities make them a good or perfect fit for a role (mentor, guide, leader), extract the speaker's judgment during construction.
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly says another person's attributes (e.g., positivity, determination) make that person well-suited for a role (mentor, guide, leader), create a relationship memory capturing the speaker's judgment and the named qualities.
Apply this to compliments and evaluative statements even if no existing memory covers the person; store the opinion as a relationship memory with the speaker as the source of the evaluation.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause was extraction skipping an explicit statement that Jon's positivity and determination make him a perfect mentor and guide, so no memory was persisted. The abstract mechanism is the construction agent failing to convert explicit evaluative statements about a person's suitability for a role into durable relational memories. This skill applies to future messages containing any explicit judgment that one person's traits qualify them for a role, regardless of topic, names, or the specific role mentioned.

payload.name: ExtractIndirectAppreciationStatements
payload.description: When a message from a speaker contains an appreciative or value-laden statement about a topic, even if phrased generically or with collective pronouns, extract a preference or event memory for that speaker.
content: During candidate extraction, treat positive evaluative statements as preference or event memories for the speaker even when they use generic phrasing (e.g., 'we', 'us', 'you') or describe a general truth; infer the speaker's own appreciation from the context.

Do not skip extraction solely because the statement lacks a first-person pronoun; attribute the attitude to the speaker whose message it is, unless the statement is an explicit quote or clearly hypothetical.

candidates.solves: The Construction Agent missed a durable memory when a speaker expressed appreciation indirectly ('Nature truly has a way of reminding us to appreciate the beauty around us'), leaving preferences incomplete. The mechanism is that extraction should infer a speaker's own attitude from collective or general statements. This applies to future messages where a speaker frames appreciation or value as a shared truth; it does not apply to quoted third-party opinions or purely hypothetical statements.

payload.name: ExtractAffirmativePossessionClaims
payload.description: When a speaker affirms having the same kind of object/gift as a previous speaker (e.g., 'I also have a ...'), extract a distinct candidate for that speaker's possession during construction.
content: During candidate extraction, when a speaker responds affirmatively to a question about possessing an item or receiving a gift (e.g., 'Yes, I also have...'), create a separate candidate for that speaker's possession/event, even if the previous speaker described a similar item.
Do not treat the affirmative reply as duplicate or redundant of the prior speaker's candidate; each speaker's fact is distinct and must produce its own memory.

candidates.solves: Extraction missed a distinct candidate when Deborah replied 'I also have a pendant' after Jolene's pendant was extracted, losing Deborah's fact. Future conversations with multiple speakers each claiming the same kind of possession/gift need a rule to produce one candidate per speaker. It does not apply to same-speaker repetition or to statements without a clear possession/attribute claim.

payload.name: Capture explicitly shared frustrations or experiences
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly says they share or understand a frustration/experience previously mentioned by another speaker, during extraction create a memory for the shared/common aspect linking both parties.
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly states they understand, share, or relate to a frustration, difficulty, or experience that another speaker previously described, create a candidate memory that captures the shared or common aspect (e.g., both speakers share this frustration) in addition to any individual memory.
Use an appropriate memory kind such as 'state' or 'relationship' to represent the shared condition, and ensure the memory references or links both participants so the commonality is preserved.

candidates.solves: During extraction, when a speaker explicitly acknowledges or shares a frustration, difficulty, or experience that another speaker previously described, the agent often records only the original speaker's individual event and drops the empathetic statement. This causes missing memories of shared experiences or common ground. The rule applies whenever a participant explicitly aligns with another's prior experience, regardless of topic, and should trigger extraction of a shared-state or relationship memory. It does not apply to implicit empathy or unstated assumptions.

payload.name: Extract shared habits for addressed person
payload.description: When a speaker addresses another person with an agreement phrase such as 'Same here, X!' or 'Me too, X!' and then mentions shared habits or states, during extraction also create a candidate for the addressed person.
content: During candidate extraction, if a speaker addresses a named person with a sharing phrase ('Same here, X!', 'Me too, X!', 'X, same here!') and lists practices, routines, or states, generate a separate candidate for the addressed person carrying those same attributes, alongside the speaker's candidate.
Keep the addressee candidate's memory kind and world_start consistent with the speaker's candidate, and do not merge speaker and addressee attributes into one memory.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction often attributes shared habits only to the speaker when they say 'Same here, X!' to another person, dropping the addressee's equivalent state; here the omission left Jolene's practices unmemorized. The abstract mechanism is direct-address agreement phrases that assert the addressee also holds the same attribute, so the rule applies to any future message where one person tells another they share a habit, routine, or state, regardless of the activity named. It does not apply when the speaker talks only about themselves without addressing the addressee.

payload.name: Extract stated feelings from multi-fact turns
payload.description: Use during extraction when a speaker's message states both a factual event/situation and the speaker's explicit feeling, assessment, or experience about it; preserve both facts.
content: During extraction, scan each speaker turn for all distinct durable facts; do not collapse the turn into a single candidate when it contains both a factual event and the speaker's explicit feeling, assessment, or experience about that event.
If both are present, emit separate candidate memories (e.g., one 'event' memory for the occurrence and one 'event'/'state' memory for the subjective experience), each citing the same source message.
Before finalizing a candidate, verify that no explicitly stated feeling or assessment in the source message is left uncaptured; include it even if it is not the main topic of the turn.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction failed because a speaker turn containing both an event fact and an explicitly stated subjective feeling was collapsed into a single event memory, dropping the feeling. The reusable mechanism is conflating multiple durable facts from one turn into one candidate. Future messages that state both an event/situation and the speaker's feelings, assessments, or experiences about it should be split into separate candidates so no stated fact is lost.

payload.name: ExtractExplicitPreferenceStatements
payload.description: During construction extraction, when a speaker explicitly states their own preference or favorite (e.g., 'my favorite', 'I love', 'I like'), extract a durable memory for that preference, even if the statement is brief or embedded in a reply.
content: During extraction, when a speaker explicitly states their own preference for a specific entity using phrases like 'my favorite', 'I love', 'I like', 'I prefer', create a separate durable memory capturing that preference.
Use memory kind 'preference' (or 'state' if preference is unavailable), set subject to the speaker, content to the preference relation, and world_start from the message timestamp.
Capture such statements even when they are brief, appear as answers to questions, or are embedded in a longer narrative about something else.
Do not apply this to hypothetical, third-party, or negated statements.

candidates.solves: An explicitly stated first-person preference in a short or embedded reply was not extracted, so no durable memory was created. The missing rule: capture direct preference statements as their own memory even when brief or embedded. This applies to any domain where a speaker favors an entity, but not to hypothetical, third-party, or negated statements.

payload.name: Preserve explicit action predicates during memory enrichment
payload.description: When updating or merging an existing memory with new evidence that states an explicit action or relation (recommends, suggests, plans, promises, gives), preserve that predicate instead of rewriting it as a preference like 'enjoys' or 'likes'.
content: During UPDATE or MERGE, if new evidence explicitly states an action or relation (e.g., recommends, suggests, plans, promises, gives) about entities already covered by the old memory, keep that predicate as a distinct clause. Do not collapse it into a different predicate (e.g., 'enjoys', 'likes', 'plays') merely because the same entities are involved.

Before enriching an existing memory, check whether the new statement's predicate matches the old memory's predicate. If they differ, either keep both predicates in the merged memory or write a separate memory for the new relation (e.g., a relationship memory 'X recommends Y to Z'). Never silently transform the new predicate to match the old one.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: an UPDATE merged explicit recommendation evidence into an older 'enjoys playing' memory, replacing 'recommends titles like' with 'particularly', so the recommendation act was lost. The abstract mechanism is predicate collapse during memory enrichment. This rule applies to any future enrichment or merge where new evidence states an explicit action or relationship (recommend, suggest, plan, promise) about items that already appear in an older memory with a different predicate.

payload.name: Preserve stated purpose in preference extraction
payload.description: When a user states a preference, plan, or goal with an explicit reason or purpose, extract that purpose into the same memory instead of storing only the surface preference.
content: During extraction, if the source message includes a preference, plan, or goal together with an explicit purpose (e.g., 'to', 'so that', 'because'), write one candidate that contains both the preference and its purpose.
When you later review existing memories for the same subject, if a memory records the preference but omits its purpose, issue an UPDATE to add the purpose rather than adding a duplicate memory.

candidates.solves: Future questions asking where or why a user wants something require the purpose that was stated alongside the preference. Extraction that stores only the preference drops that purpose and makes the memory insufficient for motivation questions. This rule applies to any statement joining a preference, plan, or goal with an explicit reason; it is not intended for event descriptions that contain no stated purpose.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Additive Preference Statements
payload.description: When a message contains a clear self-stated preference using affective language ('love', 'like', 'enjoy', 'favorite'), extract a preference memory even if it is phrased as an addition ('also', 'besides') or part of a longer reply.
content: During extraction, treat explicit self-referential preference statements as candidates for a `preference` memory whenever the speaker uses affective verbs like 'love', 'like', 'enjoy', or nouns like 'favorite'.
Do not skip a preference candidate merely because it is introduced as secondary or additive (e.g., 'also love', 'besides X I like Y', 'one of my favorites').
Extract each distinct item named as liked/loved in the message, even if multiple preferences appear in one turn, and preserve the object of the preference verb.

candidates.solves: Extraction skipped an explicit additive preference ('I also love X') because it was phrased as secondary to another item. This rule applies to any self-disclosed preference using affective language (love, like, enjoy, favorite), including 'also', 'besides', or 'one of my favorites', when the speaker is the source. It does not apply to others' preferences, hypotheticals, or retractions.

payload.name: Preserve recommendations when merging into preference memories
payload.description: When extraction or CRUD handles a candidate whose source message contains a recommendation or suggestion, keep the speech-act context distinct from mere personal preference and do not let an UPDATE/MERGE strip it.
content: During extraction, if the source explicitly recommends or suggests an entity, keep the speech-act verb (e.g., 'recommends', 'suggested') in the candidate content; do not collapse it into a bare preference like 'enjoys X'.

During CRUD, before performing an UPDATE or MERGE into an existing memory, check whether the new evidence contains a recommendation distinct from an enjoyment/preference claim. If so, preserve the recommendation explicitly (e.g., 'recommends X as ...' or 'suggested X for ...') even when merging into a preference memory, and avoid rewording it into only an enjoyed-item list.

candidates.solves: Construction often merges a new candidate containing an explicit recommendation or suggestion into an existing preference memory, converting 'recommends X as great' into 'enjoys X' and silently dropping the speech-act fact. This happens in any domain (games, books, movies, restaurants, products) whenever a source message endorses something. The rule preserves the recommendation as a distinct fact. It does not apply to pure preference statements without an explicit recommendation or suggestion.

payload.name: Extract preferences from enthusiastic activity descriptions
payload.description: Use during extraction: when a person describes an activity they engaged in with positive affect (e.g., 'awesome', 'loved', 'enjoyed'), extract a preference memory for that activity even if no explicit 'I like X' is stated.
content: During candidate extraction, treat first-person descriptions of activities performed with positive affect (e.g., 'awesome', 'loved', 'fun', 'enjoyed') as evidence of a durable preference, and create a `preference` candidate even when the message is a past-experience narrative rather than an explicit 'I like X' statement.
When a message contains multiple distinct activities, produce one candidate per activity; do not let a dominant topic (e.g., a recurring sport) suppress lesser-mentioned activities.
Do not require explicit preference wording; the enjoyment signal in the description is sufficient, provided the activity is performed by the person the memory is about.

candidates.solves: Extraction missed a user's leisure activity because it was described as an enjoyable past experience, not as 'I like X'. The mechanism is demanding explicit preference wording and attending only to the dominant topic. Treating positively-described first-person activities as preference evidence, and extracting each distinct activity, generalizes to any sport/hobby/food/media; not for neutral or third-party mentions.

payload.name: Extract explicit favorite statements as preference memories
payload.description: When a message explicitly expresses a favorite or strong preference (e.g., 'favorite', 'really into', 'love') for an entity, extract a durable preference memory preserving that intensity instead of a neutral state.
content: When a message explicitly expresses a strong preference or favorite using words like 'favorite', 'really into', 'love', or 'obsessed with' for a book, movie, show, activity, food, or other item, extract a durable 'preference' memory that names the item and preserves the positive intensity (e.g., 'X is their favorite', 'they are really into X').

Do not downgrade such a statement into a temporary state such as 'currently reading' or 'currently watching'; the preference is the durable fact. If other items are mentioned in the same message, keep the explicitly favored item in its own memory rather than merging it into a list that obscures the favorite.

candidates.solves: During extraction, explicit strong-preference statements such as 'really into X' are often downgraded to neutral states like 'currently reading X', losing the favorite fact. The rule is to preserve such statements as durable preference memories and keep the favored item distinct from other mentioned items. Applies to any future message with explicit favorite or strong-positive phrases; neutral mentions without intensity are out of scope.

payload.name: Extract pet activity preferences from owner statements
payload.description: When a user describes what their pets like to do or play, extract a preference memory during construction even if the user does not say 'I like'.
content: During candidate extraction, treat statements about a user's pets' favorite activities or games (e.g., 'they go crazy for', 'love to', 'enjoy') as preference evidence for the pet owner.
Create a preference memory linking the owner to the pet activity when the activity is recurring or habitual rather than a one-time event.
Apply this during extraction; do not wait for a later explicit preference statement.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction failed to store a directly stated fact because the preference was expressed through the user's pets rather than as a first-person 'I like' statement. The reusable failure is overlooking preference signals when the grammatical subject is a pet. Future inputs where a user describes their pets' recurring games or activities should produce a preference memory at extraction time. This does not apply to one-time pet events or statements about other people's pets.

payload.name: Preserve explicit recommendations vs preferences
payload.description: When a message contains an explicit recommendation, suggestion, or endorsement of named items, use this to preserve the recommendation relationship in memory instead of lowering it to enjoyment/preference.
content: When extracting or updating memory, if the speaker explicitly recommends, suggests, or endorses specific items (e.g., 'I recommend X', 'you should try X', 'my top pick is X'), store the recommendation claim in memory (e.g., '<speaker> recommends X,Y,Z') and preserve it during UPDATE/MERGE.

Do not collapse a recommendation into mere enjoyment: 'enjoys X' does not imply 'recommends X'. When enriching an existing memory with newly named titles, keep both clauses (recommends and enjoys) if the evidence supports both.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: an enrichment UPDATE replaced a correctly extracted recommendation claim with an enjoyment-only phrasing, so later recall about recommendations failed. Abstract mechanism: explicit recommendation is a distinct memory-worthy predicate that must survive extraction and CRUD rewrites. Applies to any future session where a speaker recommends books, games, movies, music, restaurants, or other items, especially when updating an existing preference memory.

payload.name: Extract explicit enjoyment as preference
payload.description: When a speaker uses first-person affective language like 'I love', 'I enjoy', or 'I like' about a topic or item, apply this rule.
content: During extraction, if a speaker expresses personal enjoyment or liking of a topic or item ('I love...', 'I enjoy...', 'I like...'), create a preference memory for that speaker capturing the enjoyed object; do not replace it with only a recommendation or event memory.

During CRUD updates, when enriching or updating an existing memory about the same topic, preserve and include the explicit enjoyment/preference; do not let a later recommendation or activity description overwrite or dilute it.

candidates.solves: When a speaker states personal enjoyment or liking of a topic or item using first-person affective language, the extraction stage may misclassify this as a recommendation event and lose the explicit preference. This rule requires preserving the enjoyment as a preference memory and prevents later CRUD enrichment from overwriting or diluting that preference. It applies to future sessions with similar enjoyment statements, not to third-party recommendations or actions without expressed liking.

payload.name: ExtractExplicitFirstPersonPreferences
payload.description: When a user explicitly states that something is one of their favorites or a preferred item, extract it as a preference memory even if the statement is casual or followed by other topics.
content: During extraction, treat explicit first-person statements like 'one of my favorite X is Y' or 'I love/prefer Y' as preference candidates regardless of surrounding small talk or emotional tone.
Record the stated item as a durable preference memory linked to the speaker; do not skip because the utterance also contains unrelated context.
Do not require corroborating evidence or repeated mentions when the speaker states their own preference directly.

candidates.solves: This addresses extraction-stage omissions where explicitly stated first-person preferences are skipped because the utterance is casual, emotional, or surrounded by unrelated context. It applies whenever a speaker directly names a favorite dish, activity, or item with phrasing like 'one of my favorites' or 'I love/prefer', ensuring a single explicit statement creates a durable preference memory. It does not apply to preferences inferred from behavior, mentions of others' tastes, or speculative likes.

payload.name: Extract desired attributes as separate preference memories
payload.description: When a user states characteristics of an ideal or planned place/object, extract each as its own preference memory, even if casual or embedded in other talk.
content: During extraction, when the user describes attributes of an ideal, wanted, or planned place/object (e.g., 'ideal X by the water', 'place with natural light'), create a separate `preference` memory for each attribute, stated from the user's words.
Treat casual or exclamatory statements (e.g., 'Check my...', 'Oh, I found...') as containing extractable facts; do not skip them as mere remarks.
Do not fold explicit preferences into a broad `event` or `plan` memory; keep preferences distinct so later updates cannot overwrite them.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes ignore explicitly stated preferences about a user's ideal or planned place/object when the statement is casual (e.g., 'check my ideal X by the water'), and sometimes bury such preferences inside broader event/plan memories that later updates overwrite. Future inputs that describe any desired attribute of a goal object — location, lighting, materials, size — should yield a separate, durable preference memory per attribute. This does not apply to factual past events, to attributes the user rejects, or to preferences not tied to the user's own desire.

payload.name: Extract preferences from explicit evaluative statements
payload.description: When a message contains an explicit subjective appreciation or judgment (e.g., 'X is beautiful', 'I love Y'), create a preference candidate during extraction, even if the statement is embedded in a suggestion, question, or exclamation.
content: During extraction, treat explicit evaluative language ('beautiful', 'love', 'enjoy', 'like', 'prefer', 'hate') as a preference signal and create a memory candidate for the judged object and polarity, even when it appears inside a suggestion, question, or exclamation.
Do not skip a preference just because the utterance's main purpose is another act (e.g., proposing a trip); the evaluative clause still states a durable preference.

candidates.solves: When a preference is expressed inside a suggestion or exclamation, extraction may skip it as a non-factual utterance. This rule generalizes the recognition of explicit evaluative language ('beautiful', 'love', 'like', etc.) as a preference signal regardless of the surrounding speech act, across all topics. It does not apply to inferring preferences from actions alone or neutral descriptions.

payload.name: Extract future action commitments as plan memories
payload.description: Apply during extraction when a speaker states a future action or the method for doing it, such as offering to send or deliver something.
content: During extraction, when a speaker commits to a future action or explains how they will do something (e.g., 'I can write it down and mail it'), create a plan memory candidate capturing the action and its method.
Use the `plan` memory type for any concrete future commitment; do not skip it just because the action has not happened yet.

candidates.solves: When a speaker commits to a future action or states the method by which they will accomplish it (e.g., 'I can write it down and mail it'), the extraction stage can fail to generate a candidate, leaving later questions about the plan unanswered. This skill ensures such commitments are extracted as plan memories, regardless of the action's topic. It applies to explicit statements of future action; it does not apply to preferences, past events, or vague intentions without actionable detail.

payload.name: CaptureProgressAssessmentComments
payload.description: When a speaker comments on someone's progress, effort, or success on a goal, extract it as a memory candidate even if the wording is idiomatic or informal.
content: During candidate extraction, recognize evaluative comments about a person's or project's progress (e.g., 'hard work is paying off', 'making great strides', 'coming along well') as memory-worthy statements.
Create a state memory capturing the assessment (e.g., 'X's work is paying off'), source-linked to the speaker's message, so later questions about what the speaker said about progress can be answered.
Do not skip such comments because they are idiomatic, informal, or lack an explicit subject; they are valid extraction triggers.

candidates.solves: Extraction produced no candidate for a speaker's idiomatic comment that another's hard work is 'paying off', so the fact was never stored. The gap is recognizing evaluative progress commentary as memory-worthy. This rule—capture any comment assessing progress or success, with speaker attribution—applies to future sessions where progress is discussed on any topic; it excludes compliments unrelated to progress.

payload.name: Extract stated beliefs as attributed preferences
payload.description: Apply during extraction when a speaker states a belief, opinion, or advice about what is important or effective; create a preference memory attributed to that speaker.
content: During extraction, treat explicit statements of belief, opinion, or advice as extraction candidates: if a speaker says what they think is important, effective, or the key to something, create a preference memory attributed to that speaker.
Phrase the memory as the speaker's stated belief (e.g., '<speaker> believes that <X is key to Y>'), and attach the source message link.

candidates.solves: A directly supported claim was missing because extraction skipped a statement phrased as general advice ('X is the key to Y') instead of an explicit personal preference. The rule abstracts the failure: any explicit normative statement by a speaker should become an attributed preference memory. Applies to future sessions whenever a participant expresses a belief, recommendation, or advice.

payload.name: ExtractExplicitSelfWorthStatements
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly tells the recipient what to believe about themselves (e.g., 'your worth is not defined by X') as advice or encouragement, during extraction create a candidate for that stated belief or principle instead of treating it as filler.
content: During extraction, treat explicit statements of encouragement, advice, or identity beliefs as candidate-worthy, especially when phrased as 'it's important to believe...', 'your [quality] is not defined by...', or 'you are...'. Do not skip them as mere support or filler. Extract the stated belief as a durable memory attributed to the speaker, with recipient and topic preserved, and let the CRUD stage choose the appropriate memory type.

candidates.solves: A supportive message contains an explicit belief/self-worth statement, but extraction skips it, so a later question about what the speaker said the recipient should believe is unanswerable. This guidance applies to future extraction over dialogue where one participant explicitly tells another what to believe about themselves; it excludes small talk, generic well-wishes, and utterances without explicit belief framing.

payload.name: CaptureIdiomaticCommitmentExpressions
payload.description: When a message conveys a speaker's resolve or refusal using idioms like 'not giving up' or 'won't stop', during extraction capture the underlying commitment as a memory.
content: During extraction, map idiomatic or indirect expressions of a speaker's resolve, refusal, or commitment (e.g., 'I'm not giving up', 'I won't stop', 'no quitting') to the concrete action they imply, and create a candidate memory for the speaker (type state or plan) that records the commitment or avoidance.
Do not extract when the statement is non-committal, hypothetical, or refers to someone else.

candidates.solves: The extraction stage missed a memory when a speaker used an idiomatic refusal ('I'm not giving up') instead of a literal statement ('I will not quit'). The mechanism is an over-literal parse that fails to resolve common idioms to their concrete action. This skill applies to any future message in which a speaker indirectly expresses commitment or avoidance; it does not cover hypothetical or third-party statements.

payload.name: Extract explicit motivation statements
payload.description: When a message explicitly states what motivates or drives the speaker or their group to improve, use this during extraction to persist the motivating factor as a memory.
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly states what motivates or drives them or their group (e.g., 'X pushes us to improve', 'we get better because of X'), create a memory candidate capturing the motivating factor and the behavior it drives.
Prefer a durable memory kind such as state or preference unless the statement describes a single past event; do not skip the message merely because the motivation appears within a larger reply.

candidates.solves: The failure was an extraction miss: a message stating what motivates the speaker's group was never captured, leaving later motivation questions unsupported. The mechanism is skipping explicit cause/motivation assertions during extraction. Future inputs where a speaker states what drives them or their group to improve (e.g., 'X drives us to get better') should create a memory. Does not apply to speculative third-party motives or one-off events.

payload.name: Extract habit frequency statements
payload.description: When a user describes a recurring activity with a frequency phrase (e.g., every day, twice a week, multiple times a day), extract it into a memory during candidate extraction.
content: During extraction, when a message describes a habitual or recurring activity with a frequency modifier (e.g., 'every day', 'twice a week', 'several times a day', 'very often'), create a candidate memory capturing the activity and its frequency, even if the message also contains opinions, benefits, or emotional language.

Use the `state` kind for ongoing routines (e.g., 'walks dogs multiple times a day') or `event` with a frequency qualifier when the schema distinguishes recurring events; keep the memory evidence-bound and source-linked to the message.
Do not limit extraction to purely factual or numeric statements; frequency adverbs are sufficient evidence that a routine exists and should be preserved.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is under-extraction: a clearly stated routine frequency ('multiple times a day') was omitted because the message also carried opinions. The abstract mechanism is missing habitual-frequency facts during candidate extraction. This rule transfers across topics (pets, exercise, chores) and applies whenever a user states how often a recurring activity happens, even with evaluative language; it does not apply to one-time events.

payload.name: Maintain cumulative counts for ordinal achievements
payload.description: When a user mentions an ordinal occurrence of a recurring personal achievement (first, second, third...), use this to extract and maintain a cumulative count memory and avoid overwriting earlier occurrences.
content: During extraction: whenever a message contains an ordinal indicator of a recurring achievement (first, second, third, fourth, etc.), also create a cumulative count candidate (e.g., '<subject> has achieved <ordinal> times') in addition to the individual event candidate.

During CRUD: when storing a new ordinal occurrence, add the individual event as a new memory and update the existing cumulative count memory to the stated ordinal; never UPDATE an earlier event memory to describe the new occurrence.

candidates.solves: The failure occurs when extraction records only individual ordinal events and CRUD overwrites an earlier event with a later one, so no memory ever holds the cumulative total. The reusable rule derives a cumulative count from any explicit ordinal statement of a recurring achievement and persists/updates it as a separate memory while keeping each occurrence as its own event. This applies to future sessions where a user describes repeated personal accomplishments with ordinal numbers, regardless of topic.

payload.name: Preserve Explicit Ordinal Qualifiers During Extraction
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly labels an item (e.g., creative work, project, possession) with an ordinal or other unique descriptor, apply during extraction and CRUD review to keep that qualifier in the memory.
content: During extraction, when evidence explicitly labels an entity with an ordinal or other distinguishing qualifier (e.g., 'third screenplay', 'second novel'), include that qualifier in the candidate memory's content (and subject if applicable) so the memory binds attributes to the specific instance.

During CRUD, when reviewing candidates, verify that any explicitly stated ordinal or unique descriptor is present in the memory being created or updated; if missing, fix the candidate or issue an UPDATE to attach the qualifier.

candidates.solves: When extracting memories about a person's creative works or other items that are explicitly distinguished by an ordinal (first, second, third) or another unique descriptor, extractors often preserve the attributes but drop the distinguishing qualifier, causing later queries about that specific instance to fail. This Skill instructs extractors to always retain the explicit qualifier in the memory content. It applies to any entity the speaker explicitly labels by ordinal or unique qualifier, and does not apply when the qualifier is only implicit or inferred.

payload.name: PropagateEstablishedLocationToNewEvents
payload.description: When extracting a new event for a person already known to be at a specific location from earlier context, include that location in the memory if the event occurs there and no new location is stated.
content: During extraction, before writing an event memory, check prior conversation and existing memories for an active location associated with the subject.
If the new event (e.g., an activity or discovery) continues that known stay or trip and the message gives no different location, include the established location in the extracted memory content.
Do not invent a location when the known location and the event are not connected by time or travel context.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes records an activity while dropping its location when the location is not repeated in the triggering message. This causes later factual questions about where an event happened to be unanswerable from memory. The reusable mechanism is failure to carry an established location from earlier context into newly extracted events. The rule applies to any multi-turn conversation where a subject remains in a known place and mentions subsequent events there without restating the place.

payload.name: Preserve concrete planned activities in event extractions
payload.description: When extracting a planned event or meeting, if participants explicitly propose concrete activities, items, or food/drinks to try, include those specifics in the memory instead of a generic label.
content: During extraction of a planned event or meeting, include every explicitly proposed concrete activity, item, or experience (e.g., trying fresh pastries, coffee, a specific dish) in the memory content.
If the concrete detail appears in a separate message from the meeting arrangement, combine them into one event memory rather than dropping the detail.
Use the specific nouns and verbs from the evidence; do not reduce an activity detail to a generic topic label.

candidates.solves: When extracting a planned event or meeting, the agent may summarize it with a generic label and drop explicitly proposed concrete activities or items, causing memories that only partially cover later claims. This rule applies to any plan/event extraction where participants name specific things they intend to do, eat, try, or bring; those details must be preserved even if they appear in separate messages.

payload.name: Extract-travel-location-period-facts
payload.description: When a message ties a person to a past travel or vacation location and a time period, extract a state/event candidate even if the location is mentioned in passing.
content: Create an event/state extraction candidate whenever a message associates a person with a location during a time period (e.g., a trip, vacation, visit, stay, or residence), even if that association is incidental to the message's main topic.
Resolve relative time references like 'last summer' or 'last year' to absolute dates using the message/session timestamp and record the resolved period.
When the location is a city with an unambiguous country, store both so country-level questions remain answerable.

candidates.solves: Extraction produced no candidate for a clear location-period fact ('vacation last summer in Bogota'), so it was never persisted. The missing rule is to emit state/event candidates from narrative travel/vacation mentions that tie a person, place, and time; resolve relative time to absolute dates; and include the unambiguous country. Applies to future messages containing person-location-time associations; not to hypothetical/future plans or time-less place mentions.

payload.name: Aggregate repeated location visits into count memory
payload.description: Use when a subject's visits/trips to the same city, country, or place are mentioned across multiple messages, and a memory storing the total number of visits should be created or updated.
content: When extracting candidates from a message, if the message describes a visit or trip to a location already mentioned as visited by the same subject in an existing memory, extract a candidate that records the total number of visits to that location (or updates an existing visit-count event), not only a new separate event.

During CRUD, when a candidate or existing memory contains a visit to a location and another memory records a different visit to the same location by the same subject, update or merge into one event memory that explicitly states the combined visit count.

candidates.solves: When a person's visits to the same city or country appear in more than one message, the extraction stage often records each visit as a separate event and never stores the total count, so later count questions cannot be answered from memory. This Skill instructs the agent to aggregate repeated location-visit mentions into one explicit count memory (or update an existing one), making visit-count facts durable and queryable. It applies during candidate extraction and during CRUD when merging memory candidates.

payload.name: Resolve named venue locations during extraction
payload.description: When extracting plan/event memories from messages that mention a named venue or franchise with well-known locations, include those possible locations (e.g., states) explicitly.
content: During extraction, if a message mentions a named destination (e.g., theme park, stadium, landmark, chain) whose geographic location(s) are widely known, include the resolved location(s) (e.g., 'California or Florida') in the candidate content, even if the user did not state them. If the venue has multiple known sites, list the possible states explicitly. Only use well-established facts; avoid speculative or obscure inferences.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause: extraction captured a plan to visit a named theme park but omitted the park's well-known geographic locations, leaving a later location query unsupported. The reusable mechanism is that named venues or franchises carry established location facts that should be included in extracted plan/event memories. Future inputs mentioning any well-known destination—theme parks, stadiums, landmarks, or chains—should trigger this location-resolving rule.

payload.name: Extract how the user discovered an event as a separate memory
payload.description: When a user states how they heard about or discovered an event, place, or opportunity (saw a flyer, friend referral, online ad), extract that discovery as its own memory candidate during extraction.
content: During extraction, when the user explicitly states how they learned about an event or opportunity (e.g., saw a flyer, heard from a friend, found an ad), create a separate event memory capturing the discovery source, in addition to any memory of the event itself.
Set memory_kind to 'event', subject to the speaker, and world_start to the session timestamp; include the concrete source and place (e.g., 'at the local pet store').
Keep discovery-source memories distinct from the main event memory; do not merge them, so future questions such as 'How did X hear about Y?' have supporting evidence.

candidates.solves: The extraction stage recorded the workshop enrollment and a related meeting but omitted the user's explicit statement that she saw a workshop flyer at her local pet store, so 'how did she hear about it' became unanswerable.
