The reusable pattern is that any explicit disclosure of a discovery source (flyer, referral, advertisement, online post) for an event or opportunity is a distinct durable fact that should be extracted independently whenever such a statement appears. It does not apply to opinions, preferences, or details already fully captured by an existing memory.

payload.name: Extract all explicitly stated plan elements
payload.description: When a plan or event is described across multiple messages, retrieve this Skill to ensure each explicitly named activity or detail is captured during candidate extraction.
content: During extraction, treat each explicitly stated element of a plan or event (activity, item, time, participant) as an extractable fact, even if it appears in an earlier message than the message that most clearly names the plan.

When multiple messages jointly describe one plan, either include all explicitly mentioned elements in a single candidate's content or create one candidate per element; never let a later, more prominent mention cause earlier distinct details to be omitted.

candidates.solves: When multiple messages jointly define a plan, extraction may keep only the later salient message and drop earlier explicit elements, causing supported claims to be missing from memory. The rule requires persisting all explicitly named elements of a plan, not just the last mention. It applies to future sessions where several messages together state a plan's components, but not to inferring unstated details.

payload.name: Extract explicit relationship-framing statements
payload.description: When a user explicitly states a view or relationship framing about someone or something (e.g., 'they are family', 'I see her as my child'), capture that framing as a memory during extraction.
content: During extraction, treat explicit declarative statements that frame an entity's role or relationship (e.g., 'X are family', 'I consider Y like a sibling', 'my pet is my baby') as memory-worthy content.
Create a profile or relationship memory recording the stated view or framing, even when the same message also contains concrete events or activities.
Do not require action-oriented evidence; a clear statement of how a user regards someone or something is durable information that should be extracted independently.

candidates.solves: Extraction omitted an explicit user statement ('pets are family') because it focused on concrete events and photo-sharing, so the belief never entered memory. The reusable mechanism is overlooking declarative statements that frame an entity's role or belonging. Applies whenever a future message explicitly states a view or relationship framing about a person, pet, or object, independent of the topic or the presence of concurrent event details.

payload.name: Extract photo-shared object descriptions
payload.description: When a user indicates sharing a picture and then gives a short descriptive phrase about the shown item, extract the description as a memory.
content: When a user shares a photo and then gives a brief evaluative description of the shown item (e.g., an adjective phrase), preserve that description in memory.
Resolve the item from context (including pronouns) and store the description as a state or preference memory.

candidates.solves: When a user shares a photo and then describes the pictured object with a short adjective phrase, the construction stage may skip extraction because the sentence is elliptical and the object is only implied. This rule ensures such photo-plus-description statements are captured as memory candidates, so later questions about the user's description can be answered.

payload.name: Extract pet-ownership memories from possessive pet references
payload.description: When a speaker refers to 'my dog', 'family's cat', 'our pet', or shares a photo of a pet, treat it as evidence they have or had that pet and extract a state/event memory.
content: During extraction, when a message contains a possessive reference to a pet (e.g., my dog, our cat, my family's dog) or describes a pet in a photo or memory, create a candidate memory that the speaker has or had that pet; use 'state' for current ownership and 'event' for childhood or past experiences.
Do not generate a pet-ownership memory from desire or hypothetical statements alone (e.g., 'I wish I had a dog'); only when the pet is presented as real or past-owned.

candidates.solves: The construction agent failed to extract a speaker's pet-ownership memory from an indirect possessive reference ('my family's dog'), even though it extracted from another speaker's explicit pet story. The abstract mechanism is that possessive or photo-based pet mentions are treated as non-factual or overlooked, when they are direct evidence of having or having had a pet. This rule applies to any future message where a speaker mentions a pet via possessive language or shared photo/memory, and ensures both current and childhood pet ownership facts are captured.

payload.name: Extract explicit object identification from user answers
payload.description: Use when a user message explicitly identifies an object they possess or have shown; during extraction, create object possession and, if applicable, sharing event candidates.
content: When a user message explicitly states what an object is (e.g., 'It's a map of Middle-earth from LOTR'), always extract a candidate memory that the speaker possesses/owns that object, storing the identifying details.
If the message or surrounding turns indicate the object was shown, given, or otherwise shared with another person, also extract an event candidate for that sharing action.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that the extraction stage produced no candidate from a user message that directly identified an object ('It's a map of Middle-earth from LOTR'), so the whole claim was lost. The rule generalizes to any future message where a speaker explicitly names an object they own or have shown, ensuring such clear identifiers are always turned into memories; it does not apply when no object is identifiable or when the message is unrelated to possessions/events.

payload.name: Capture explicit photo-sharing in extraction
payload.description: When a message uses a deictic sharing phrase like 'Here are ...' while presenting something the speaker created, extract the event of sharing a photo of that creation, not only the creation itself.
content: During extraction, if the speaker uses a first-person deictic sharing phrase such as 'Here are ...' or 'Here is ...' to present something they made, treat the act of sharing a photo or visual of that creation as a distinct durable event fact.
When writing the event memory, include both the creation and the explicit photo-sharing act; do not reduce the candidate to only the creation, recipe, or mix-ins.
Only include photo-sharing when the message explicitly indicates a visual was shared (e.g., 'Here are some ... that I made'); do not infer a photo from mere descriptions of the item.

candidates.solves: During extraction from conversational messages, when a speaker uses a first-person deictic sharing phrase such as 'Here are ...' to present something they created, extractors often record the creation or recipe but omit that the speaker shared a photo of it. This rule applies to future messages where a visual-sharing phrase accompanies a described creation (made food, built object, etc.), and instructs extractors to record the photo-sharing act as a durable event fact. It does not apply when no visual-sharing phrase is present or when sharing a photo is merely implied rather than stated.

payload.name: Extract explicit personal-meaning statements from keepsakes
payload.description: Apply during extraction when a user explicitly says an object, photo, or keepsake reminds them of a person, feeling, or memory.
content: During extraction, when the user explicitly states what a personal object, photo, or keepsake reminds them of (e.g., 'this picture reminds me of ...'), create a candidate memory capturing that meaning as a durable state or relationship, even if the object was mentioned earlier or appears incidental.

Do not require an additional cue or question; an explicit 'reminds me of' statement is sufficient evidence to extract. If the statement connects the object to a person, prefer a relationship memory; if it expresses a feeling or value, use state.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction missed explicit statements where users disclose the personal significance of objects or keepsakes, so later recall questions were unsupported. This rule generalizes to any future session where a user explicitly describes what something reminds them of; apply it to capture such meaning statements during extraction.

payload.name: Extract user-owned objects and their personal meaning
payload.description: When a user message explicitly describes an object the user owns and the personal reminder or meaning it holds, extract a memory recording the object and its significance.
content: During extraction, when the speaker explicitly says they own or keep an object and states what it reminds them to do or be, create a memory candidate that records both the object and the stated personal meaning (e.g., as a state or preference). Do not skip it because the wording describes a reminder or feeling rather than an event.
Treat such statements as durable facts about the user even if the object is fictional or cultural; capture the user's own stated purpose, not general knowledge about the object.

candidates.solves: The diagnosis shows no memory candidate was extracted from an explicit statement about a personal painting and its reminder, causing a missing fact. The failure mechanism is under-extraction of self-disclosed owned objects with personal meaning. This Skill applies to future questions where a user describes an item and the value it holds; it does not apply to statements about others' objects or to general knowledge.

payload.name: Preserve picture sharing as event instead of ownership
payload.description: When a message states that someone shared, posted, or sent a picture and then describes what it depicts or who created it, apply this during extraction to preserve the sharing as an event instead of converting it into an ownership fact.
content: During extraction, when a speaker says they shared, posted, or sent a picture, photo, or image, record a memory that captures the sharing action as an event, including what the picture shows or its creator when stated.
Do not rewrite 'shared a picture of X by Y' into 'owns an X created by Y' or 'has an X-themed Y'; sharing a picture does not imply ownership of the depicted object.
If the message describes the picture's content or creator, keep that as part of the event description rather than creating a separate possession/state memory about the depicted object.

candidates.solves: Extraction often conflates 'shared a picture of X made by Y' with 'owns X made by Y', losing the sharing event. This candidate instructs extractors to record the sharing action as an event and keep the depicted object/creator as event detail, not as a possession state. Applies to any future message where a user shares a photo, image, or picture and describes its contents or provenance.

payload.name: Extract Explicit User-Stated Views
payload.description: When a user explicitly states how they view or regard something (e.g., 'feel like', 'view as', 'is like'), during extraction, capture that stated view as a candidate memory.
content: During extraction, when the user explicitly states how they view or regard an object (phrases such as 'feel like', 'view as', 'treat as', 'is like'), create a candidate memory that records the stated view.
Use a 'relationship' memory when the view connects the user to an object (e.g., user views X as family); otherwise use 'preference' for attitudes toward the object.

candidates.solves: Extraction misses explicit statements where the user states how they view or regard something (e.g., 'pets feel like family') because the phrasing is comparative or identity-like rather than a direct assertion. The rule is to treat any explicit user statement of their own attitude or way of viewing an object as an extraction candidate, captured as a relationship or preference. This applies whenever the user directly expresses a view about people, pets, objects, or abstract ideas; it does not apply to inferred opinions from behavior, habits, or third-party statements.

payload.name: Extract implied death from euphemistic language
payload.description: When extracting or updating memories, if a message implies a person is deceased through phrases like 'will never be able to...' or 'I miss him/her here', record the person as deceased or likely deceased instead of softening to a vague ability-based state.
content: During extraction, when a message strongly implies a person is deceased through phrases like 'will never be able to...', 'I miss him/her here', 'passed away', or 'is no longer with us', record the person's death as a durable state (e.g., subject is deceased) or event, rather than a softened paraphrase such as 'no longer able to support'.
Only infer death from clear euphemistic/loss language; do not infer from mere absence, distance, or 'I miss you' to someone who could still be alive.

During CRUD, when editing or merging memories, preserve or add an explicit deceased/likely-deceased state when the source evidence supports it, and avoid replacing it with vague ability-based phrasing.

candidates.solves: Extraction (and CRUD updates) often soften euphemistic or indirect references to death into vague states like 'no longer able to support', losing the key fact that the person is likely deceased. This skill instructs agents to recognize strong death-implying phrases and store an explicit deceased/likely deceased state linked to the person, applicable to any conversation where a user mourns or references someone in a way that clearly implies they have died.

payload.name: Preserve co-participants in joint events
payload.description: When extracting an event, plan, or activity from a message using first-person plural (we/our) and context establishes a partner, spouse, or family, attribute it to the group, not just the speaker.
content: During extraction, when a message uses first-person plural (e.g., 'we', 'our') to describe an event, plan, or activity, include the co-participants implied by the context (e.g., established partner, spouse, or family) in the memory content rather than attributing the activity to the speaker alone.
Use the established relationship term (partner, family, etc.) when the co-participant's name is not stated; do not invent names or relationships not present in the conversation.

candidates.solves: The extraction candidate for a family get-together recorded only Evan, dropping his partner implied by 'we', so the memory could not support how Evan spends time with his bride. This generalizes to any joint event or plan expressed with first-person plural where a companion or group is established. Applies to future extractions of shared activities, plans, and events in any topic; do not apply when 'we' is editorial or co-participants are unsupported by context.

payload.name: Extract speaker actions in shared activities
payload.description: When a message describes an activity shared with others (playdates, classes, group events) and states what the user does as well as what others or pets do, extract the user's own action as a distinct fact; do not summarize only the group or others' actions.
content: During extraction, when a message describes a shared activity and explicitly states what the user does (e.g., chats, watches, helps) alongside what others or pets do, include the user's own action in the candidate content as a distinct fact; do not let the candidate capture only the other participants' experience or the group activity.
When the candidate will UPDATE or MERGE an existing memory, ensure the new content preserves the speaker-action detail even if the existing memory already records the shared activity itself.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates for shared activities often keep only what the other participants or pets did, dropping the user's own explicitly stated behavior, so later questions about the user's role fail. This rule applies to any message describing a joint event (playdates, classes, meetups, group outings) where the user states their own action alongside others' actions: candidates must record the user's action as a distinct fact, and updates/merges must preserve it. It does not apply when the message describes only others' actions with no stated user involvement.

payload.name: Extract bonding shared-activity memories from informal descriptions
payload.description: When a message describes a past or current shared activity with a named person and explicitly ties it to bonding, memories, or closeness, extract a candidate even if the activity is described informally; map to the conventional activity the context implies.
content: During extraction, treat statements where the speaker says they did/do an activity with another person and calls it a way to bond, make memories, or grow closer as high-value event/relationship candidates, even when the activity is named generically (e.g., 'play games', 'gaming').

When the context unambiguously implies a conventional activity ('gaming' → video games, 'cards' → card games), extract that specific activity; otherwise record the activity at the level of specificity actually stated.
Do not fabricate relationship details or durations beyond the message; link the memory to the named person and keep the bonding/memories purpose as part of the memory evidence.

candidates.solves: Addresses extraction misses where a user describes a past shared activity with a partner or relative in informal terms and ties it to bonding/memories, leaving later questions unsupported. The rule requires generating a candidate from the clearly implied conventional activity rather than an explicit noun. Applies to relational activity statements across topics; not to hypothetical mentions or labels unsupported by context.

payload.name: ExtractExplicitSharedEnjoyedActivity
payload.description: When a message explicitly states that two people enjoy doing an activity together, use this to create a relationship or state memory candidate during extraction.
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly and in first person describes an activity they enjoy doing with another person (e.g., 'we have a great time doing X', 'we love to X together'), create a candidate memory capturing that shared activity as a state or relationship.
Treat such a clear statement as sufficient evidence; do not require repeated mentions or an explicit 'fact' framing. Ensure the candidate includes both people and the activity.

candidates.solves: This addresses extraction-stage omissions where an explicit statement about two people enjoying a shared activity is committed but never converted into a memory candidate, leaving the fact permanently missing. The abstraction covers any first-person, unambiguous description of a shared pastime or activity; it does not apply to vague mentions, third-party reports, or statements that merely describe a one-time event without indicating enjoyment.

payload.name: Preserve joint participants in event extraction
payload.description: When extracting an event, if the source message explicitly states or clearly implies additional participants (e.g., 'my partner and I', 'we', 'together with X'), include all participants in the memory content instead of attributing the event only to the speaker.
content: During event extraction, preserve every participant explicitly named or clearly implied in the source (e.g., 'my partner and I traveled', 'we went', 'together with X'). Do not reduce a collective event to the speaker alone.

When the additional participant is a recurring person (e.g., partner, spouse, family member), include their role or identity in the event memory so future queries about joint activities remain answerable.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: event extraction dropped a co-participant ('my partner') from a joint travel event, so later queries about the shared activity were unanswerable. This is a general mechanism: when a source explicitly or implicitly names multiple participants, reducing the event to the speaker alone discards durable facts. The rule applies to future event extractions in any domain where messages describe joint activities, and should be applied during candidate extraction.

payload.name: Preserve shared activities from plural statements
payload.description: When a user message uses first-person plural (we/us/our) to describe an activity, preference, or experience, extract it and keep the companion in the memory.
content: During extraction, treat brief first-person plural statements (we/us/our) about activities, preferences, or experiences as candidate-worthy; do not skip them in favor of longer or seemingly richer messages.

When such a statement describes a shared activity, preserve the shared nature and any companion identifiable from context (e.g., spouse, partner, friend) in the memory content instead of attributing the activity only to the speaker.
If who 'we' refers to is unclear from prior context, record the activity as shared without inventing a specific companion.

candidates.solves: Users often describe shared activities or preferences with first-person plural pronouns. The extraction stage may skip these brief statements or store them without the companion, producing incomplete relational memories. This skill ensures plural-subject statements are selected as candidates and that the shared nature and identifiable companion are preserved, applying to any conversation where a user mentions doing something with a partner, spouse, friend, or family member.

payload.name: ExtractExplicitSuggestionsAsMemoryCandidates
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly suggests or recommends a specific action for another person or their possessions during conversation, extract it as a memory candidate.
content: During extraction, treat explicit suggestions or recommendations (e.g., 'I'd put X on your Y', 'You should try Z') as durable memory candidates even if the addressee has not agreed or acted on them.
Preserve the source (speaker), target (addressee/object), and the proposed action using an allowed memory kind such as plan or event.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction often skips explicit suggestions or recommendations because they are not stated as settled facts or preferences. The diagnosed mechanism: the agent produced no candidates for a direct suggestion, losing an answerable fact. This rule makes the agent capture any explicit recommendation as a durable, source-linked memory, applying to future sessions where one person advises another about an action or object.

payload.name: Extract explicit status assertions as state candidates
payload.description: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly states the current condition or status of an entity (person, business, project), generate a state candidate even if the statement is brief or in casual conversation.
content: During extraction: when a message explicitly states the current status or condition of an entity (e.g., doing well, struggling, open, closed, on track), create a 'state' candidate linked to that entity and the message, even if the statement is brief or embedded in casual conversation.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure was that a short explicit status update ('the store's doing great') produced no extraction candidate, so the fact never entered memory. The abstract mechanism is under-extraction of clear state assertions when they appear in casual or small-talk turns. This rule applies to any future message containing an explicit current-status statement about any entity, and ensures such facts are promoted to state memories regardless of brevity or conversational context. It does not apply to opinions, future intentions, or statements requiring inference.

payload.name: Preserve Attribution of Group/Instructor Emphasis
payload.description: Apply during extraction and updates when a message attributes an emphasis, teaching, rule, or belief to a class, instructor, group, or organization: keep that entity as the subject rather than shifting the claim to the speaker's personal preference.
content: When a source message attributes an emphasis, teaching, rule, or belief to a class, instructor, group, or organization (e.g., 'the instructor stresses X', 'the class emphasizes Y'), keep that entity as the subject of the memory content; record what the entity teaches or emphasizes, not only the speaker's personal experience or enjoyment of it.

During both extraction and CRUD, when merging details from a message into an existing memory, preserve the original attribution of statements; if the memory currently only records the speaker's perspective, add the entity-level claim as a separate, clearly attributed fact.

candidates.solves: During extraction, a claim about what a painting class/instructor emphasizes was rewritten as the speaker's personal preference, losing the attribution and breaking later retrieval of the class's emphasis. The reusable mechanism is subject-shifting from a third-party attribution to the speaker; this rule applies to any future message reporting what an instructor, class, group, or organization teaches, stresses, or believes, preserving evidence-linked attribution.

payload.name: Preserve explicit reasons for actions and decisions
payload.description: When a message states a decision or action and explicitly gives reasons or motivations, include those reasons in the memory candidate so 'why' questions can be answered later.
content: When a message states a decision or action and explicitly gives reasons or motivations (e.g., 'because', 'felt like', 'was fascinated by'), include those reasons in the same memory candidate or as an additional memory, so the 'why' is preserved.

Before finalizing an extraction candidate, check whether the source sentence answers 'why did this happen?' If yes, the reason should appear in the memory content; do not replace it with only the event and its consequences.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates often preserve the fact of an action or decision but drop the explicitly stated reasons or motivations, so later 'why' questions cannot be answered. This skill applies whenever a message contains an action/decision plus explicit reasons; the constructed memory must preserve both. It does not apply to reasons that are only implied or unsupported by the message.

payload.name: Extract explicit advice as memory candidates
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly gives advice, recommendation, or guidance to another person in the conversation, extract it as a memory candidate.
content: During extraction, if a message contains explicit advice, recommendation, or guidance from one speaker to another (e.g., 'you should', 'keep trying'), create a candidate that records the advice content, giver, and recipient when identifiable.
Use an allowed memory kind (such as event for the act of advising) and include the topic being advised on.
Link the candidate to the source message so the memory is evidence-bound and traceable.

candidates.solves: The extraction stage skipped an explicit advice message, so the advice never entered memory. This is a general gap: prescriptive statements from one speaker to another ('you should', 'keep trying') are not extracted as candidates. Apply when a future message contains such explicit advice; preserve the advice, giver, recipient, and source. Do not apply to implicit hints, agent instructions, or already-covered advice.

payload.name: ExtractDirectRequestsAsEvents
payload.description: Use during construction extraction when a message contains an explicit request or question from one person asking another for help or action on a specific topic.
content: When a message contains an explicit request or ask from one person to another for help, information, or action on a specific topic, extract an 'event' memory that directly states the request: who asked, whom they asked, what they asked about, and when. Do not let a paraphrase of the underlying need, struggle, or future intention replace the explicit request.

If the same message also contains a broader need or plan, both may be extracted as separate memories, but the direct ask must have its own memory so later questions like 'what did X ask Y for?' can be answered.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: extraction paraphrased an explicit request into a general need, so the ask itself was never stored. The reusable mechanism is that direct requests are often reduced to their underlying motivation, losing the request act. This skill preserves explicit asks as event memories whenever a speaker directly asks another for help on a topic; it does not apply to implied needs or statements lacking a direct ask.

payload.name: Extract explicit advice between speakers
payload.description: When during extraction one speaker explicitly suggests, recommends, or advises a course of action to another speaker, create a candidate memory for that suggestion even if phrased tentatively.
content: During extraction, treat explicit advice, recommendations, or suggestions from one speaker to another as durable, memory-worthy facts even when phrased tentatively (e.g., 'Maybe look into...', 'Consider...', 'You might try...').
Create a candidate memory capturing the adviser, the recipient, and the advised action so the suggestion can be retrieved later.

candidates.solves: During extraction, explicit suggestions or recommendations that one speaker gives to another were missed, so the fact was never stored and later questions about the advice could not be answered. The reusable mechanism is that advice phrased tentatively ('Maybe look into...', 'You should try...') is still a durable fact about the relationship between participants. This rule applies to any future session where a participant gives advice to another and a later question may ask about it.

payload.name: Capture explicit suggestions as memory candidates
payload.description: When a message contains an explicit suggestion, recommendation, or advice from one speaker to another about a specific item, book, action, or resource, extract it as a memory candidate during candidate extraction.
content: During candidate extraction, treat explicit suggestions, recommendations, or advice from one conversation participant to another as durable, queryable facts. Capture the speaker, the recipient, and the suggested item or action (e.g., 'Evan suggested Sam check out a dream interpretation book'). Do not skip such statements because they are phrased as advice or suggestions; record them as event or relationship memories.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that extraction generated no candidate for an explicit suggestion from one speaker to another, leaving the fact absent from memory. The failure mechanism is that recommendations and advice phrased as suggestions were not recognized as durable, queryable facts during extraction. The proposed rule abstracts this by treating explicit suggestions as memory-worthy events or relationships regardless of topic, so future questions about who suggested or recommended what can be answered.

payload.name: Extract stated future plans or aspirations as plan memories
payload.description: When a message contains an explicit statement of a speaker's possible future action or aspiration (e.g., 'Maybe I'll...', 'I want to...', 'I plan to...'), create a separate `plan` memory for that statement during extraction, even if the message also yields other memories.
content: During extraction, scan each message for clauses where the speaker states a possible future action, goal, or aspiration (e.g., 'Maybe I'll...', 'I might...', 'I want to...', 'I plan to...').
For each such stated intention, generate a separate `plan` candidate with the speaker as subject, even if the same message yields other candidates (invitations, current activities, etc.).
Do not fold the aspiration into a broader event or preference memory; keep it as its own durable, evidence-bound memory linked to the source message.

candidates.solves: Extraction can omit a speaker's explicit future aspiration when the same message also yields candidates about other topics, leaving that claim unsupported; treat every stated plan or intention ('Maybe I'll...', 'I want to...', 'I plan to...') as its own `plan` candidate. This applies to future messages with explicit first-person intentions, not to historical events or mere hypotheticals without a stated intention.

payload.name: Extract explicit advice between speakers
payload.description: When a message contains direct advice or recommendation from one person to another, generate a candidate memory during extraction.
content: During extraction, if a message contains an explicit piece of advice or recommendation from one speaker to another (signaled by phrases like 'make sure you', 'you should', 'I advise you', 'you need to'), create a candidate memory recording the advice, the advisor, the recipient, and the topic or goal of the advice.
Treat a single explicit statement as sufficient for a durable memory; do not require repetition across turns.

candidates.solves: The construction pipeline failed to generate any extraction candidate from a message that contained clear, explicit advice from one speaker to another, so the fact never entered memory. The abstract mechanism is an extraction omission for advice-bearing statements. A rule that detects and extracts explicit advice from any message reliably preserves such relationship facts for future questions, regardless of topic.

payload.name: Extract current activity from pleasantry-prefixed statements
payload.description: When extracting from a user message that begins with thanks, greetings, or other filler but then explicitly states what they are currently doing, writing about, or working on, use this Skill.
content: During extraction, do not skip a message merely because it opens with thanks or a pleasantry.
If the remainder explicitly describes the user's current ongoing activity, interest, or work topic, generate a compact state memory capturing that activity.
Keep the memory general, source-linked, and free of conversational filler.

candidates.solves: During extraction, explicit self-disclosures of current activities or interests can be missed when they appear after conversational pleasantries such as thanks. This Skill ensures that when a user states what they are currently doing or writing about, a compact state memory is extracted despite surrounding filler, transferring across topics like writing, work projects, hobbies, or studies.

payload.name: Preserve advice tips when extracting alongside offers
payload.description: Use when a speaker's message contains specific tips or strategies, possibly with an offer of help; preserve the concrete advice in memory, not just the offer or plan.
content: During extraction, when a message contains specific tips, strategies, or methods, capture those concrete advice items in the memory candidate content even if the message also contains an offer to help or a plan.
Prefer a candidate that states what the advice was (e.g., the strategies shared) over one that only records the offer; if both are durable, include the tips in the same or a separate candidate.

candidates.solves: Extraction failures occur when a message bundles concrete advice with an offer: the candidate records only the meta-offer (e.g., offering a plan) and drops the substantive tips. This rule applies to future messages where a speaker shares actionable strategies (study, time management, health, etc.) with or without an accompanying offer; it ensures the tips themselves are stored so later recall can cite them.

payload.name: Extract explicit approach-to-challenges statements
payload.description: When a message explicitly states how the speaker or their group handles tough situations or challenges (strategy, attitude, or mutual support), use this Skill during extraction.
content: During extraction, if a message contains an explicit statement describing how the speaker or their group responds to challenges (e.g., backing each other up, not quitting, improving), generate a candidate memory capturing that approach as a state or preference.
Do not require the statement to be the main topic; extract it even when embedded in a longer reply that also mentions past events.
Link the candidate to the speaker's profile or group relationship, and record the source message and timestamp for provenance.

candidates.solves: The extraction stage produced no candidates for an explicit statement describing how the speaker's group handles difficult situations. Future inputs may contain similar statements about coping strategies, teamwork approaches, or attitudes toward challenges. This skill ensures such explicit approach descriptions are extracted as durable memory candidates, rather than being skipped. It applies to messages where a speaker states how they or their group deal with adversity; it does not apply to purely factual or transient statements that do not describe an approach or attitude.

payload.name: Extract routine steps and assessments
payload.description: When a speaker directly describes how they do or manage something (a routine, process, or care procedure), extract each concrete step and overall assessment as separate candidate memories.
content: During candidate extraction, when a speaker describes how they do or manage something (care routine, preparation, maintenance, or any recurring process), capture each distinct step, requirement, or stated fact as its own candidate claim.
Do not skip such descriptions because they appear easy, obvious, or generic; each concrete component is evidence worth storing.
Also extract overall assessments the speaker makes about the routine (e.g., whether it is difficult or enjoyable) as separate candidate claims.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause was that extraction produced no candidates from a speaker's direct description of a routine (cleaning, feeding, lighting), leaving the pipeline with nothing to store. The abstract mechanism is that concrete procedural answers were treated as not memorable, possibly because they seemed simple or generic. This skill applies to any future message where a speaker enumerates steps or requirements for a routine they perform, regardless of topic; it is not meant for hypothetical instructions or for claims without speaker grounding.

payload.name: Extract explicit advice and suggestions from conversation
payload.description: When a message contains an explicit suggestion, recommendation, or advice from one speaker to another, extract a candidate memory even if the language is conversational or motivational.
content: During extraction, when a message contains an explicit suggestion, recommendation, or advice from one person to another (including encouragement like 'keep trying new things'), generate a candidate memory that records the advice, the recipient, and the source speaker. Do not discard it because it is conversational or phrased as motivational language.

Represent the advice with an allowed memory kind that fits the semantics—use 'plan' for actionable recommendations directed at the recipient, or 'event' for the act of advising—and always bind the candidate to the source message for evidence.

candidates.solves: Extraction sometimes misses explicit advice when phrased as conversational encouragement (e.g., 'keep trying new things'). The fix is to extract any explicit recommendation from one speaker to another as a candidate, regardless of tone. This applies to future messages containing clear suggestions or advice, but not to implied or non-actionable statements.

payload.name: PreserveExplicitValueClaimsInExtraction
payload.description: When extracting memory candidates, if a speaker states a specific value, belief, goal, or influential lesson, preserve the exact detail in the memory content instead of reducing it to a generic theme summary.
content: During extraction, when a message explicitly states a specific value, belief, goal, or lesson (e.g., 'my mom stressed the value of helping others'), include the concrete claim and its source in the memory content; do not replace it with a generic phrase like 'influence of loved ones' or 'shared values'.

If a speaker's message covers both a broad theme and a named specific detail, keep the named detail; a memory that only summarizes the conversation theme is insufficient for future queries about that specific fact.
Attribute the specific claim to the correct person/source in the memory so it remains evidence-bound and traceable.

candidates.solves: The extraction candidate over-generalized a message containing an explicit value statement into a generic summary about values and loved ones, dropping the queryable fact. The abstract mechanism is that broad conversational themes can overshadow concrete personal statements during candidate generation. The rule—preserve explicitly named values/beliefs/goals and their sources in memory content—applies to any future extraction where a message mixes a theme with a specific claim that a later question may target.

payload.name: Extract offers from polite closing phrases
payload.description: When a speaker offers help, support, tips, or assistance within a polite closing phrase, use during extraction to create a candidate capturing the offer.
content: During extraction, recognize explicit offers of help, support, tips, or assistance even when they appear in polite closings like 'if you need anything, just let me know'; extract the offer as a memory candidate, including what was offered and to whom.
Do not let the courtesy framing suppress the underlying commitment; an offer is an event or relational fact even if phrased as an afterthought.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause was an explicit offer of support being omitted during extraction because it was embedded in a polite closing phrase, so the fact never reached memory. Similar omissions occur whenever a speaker offers concrete help, tips, or assistance as a courteous afterthought. This rule applies during extraction to any message containing a clear offer of assistance regardless of topic; it does not apply to vague pleasantries that contain no actual offer.

payload.name: Preserve explicit qualifiers in advice extraction
payload.description: When constructing memories from messages that give advice, instructions, or tips, if the source contains explicit qualifiers for manner, pace, or attitude, preserve them in extracted candidates and final memory content.
content: During extraction from advice/instruction messages, keep all explicit qualifiers and attitude words (e.g., slowly, gently, patiently, positively) in the candidate text; do not paraphrase them away into broader synonyms.

During CRUD, before accepting an ADD or UPDATE, verify that the memory content retains every essential qualifier present in the source message; if any is missing, revise the content or create a supplementary memory entry.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates that paraphrase advice can drop explicit qualifiers of manner, pace, or attitude, leaving memories that only partially support later recall. The reusable rule is to preserve all such explicit qualifiers when creating memories from advice or instruction messages, since future questions may ask for those exact details. This applies to any future advice/instruction exchange across topics; it does not apply when the memory intentionally records only a high-level theme or when the qualifier is redundant.

payload.name: Extract hedged future proposals as plan memories
payload.description: When a speaker directly states or proposes a future activity using tentative or conditional phrasing (e.g., 'maybe we can', 'let's', 'I'd love to'), during extraction treat it as a plan memory.
content: During extraction, create a plan memory for any explicit future intention or proposal, even when hedged with 'maybe', 'could', 'would love', 'let's', or similar tentative wording.
Record the actor, the activity, and any co-participant or location if stated. Resolve future time relative to the message/session timestamp when possible, otherwise leave it unspecified.
Only extract when the speaker directly states the intention; do not extrapolate from indirect or non-explicit context.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: an explicit but tentatively phrased future proposal received no extraction candidates, so the plan was lost. The abstract mechanism is that future intentions and suggestions are plan memories regardless of hedging. Supported by the message's direct statement of intent. Applies to any future message where a speaker proposes or states a future activity with someone, across topics.

payload.name: Preserve explicit motivational statements as memory facts
payload.description: When a source message explicitly states what motivates, drives, or keeps a speaker going, capture that stated reason as a distinct memory fact.
content: During extraction, if the speaker explicitly states a motivation or reason that keeps them going (e.g., 'it's knowing that ... that keeps me going', 'I write because ...'), include that exact motivational claim as a distinct clause in the candidate memory; do not replace it with a generic summary of the activity or feelings.

During CRUD, when enriching or updating an existing memory, verify that any explicit motivation in the source message is present in the new version; if it is missing, add it to the enriched content rather than letting it be absorbed into a broader paraphrase.

candidates.solves: Extraction sometimes summarizes what a speaker does and feels but drops the explicit stated reason for persisting (e.g., 'keeps me going'), leaving later motivation/values questions unanswered. This Skill applies when a message contains an explicit first-person motivation phrase ('keeps me going', 'what motivates me', 'I do X because'), and does not apply to inferred or hypothetical reasons. It instructs preserving the stated reason as a distinct memory fact during extraction and checking during CRUD that updates do not discard it.

payload.name: Preserve notable direct quotes as verbatim memories
payload.description: When a message contains a distinctive, pithy, or emotionally salient direct quotation that a future question could ask about, create a memory that preserves the exact wording.
content: During extraction, identify direct quotations that are distinctive or memorable (e.g., a toast, motto, promise, or exact phrasing about a key event).
For such quotes, create an event or statement memory capturing the verbatim wording, attributed to the speaker and linked to the message.
Do not replace abstract summaries; add the quote memory alongside them so both gist and exact wording are retained.
Skip routine, trivial, or highly verbose statements where the exact wording is unlikely to be queried.

candidates.solves: Extraction often paraphrases direct quotes into abstract summaries, losing exact wording that future questions may require. Apply when a message contains a distinctive or memorable quotation (toast, promise, motto, striking phrase) about a key event or relationship; persist the verbatim quote as a memory alongside any abstract summary. Do not apply to routine, trivial, or highly verbose statements.

payload.name: ExtractDurationFromRelationshipStatements
payload.description: When a speaker states a duration (e.g., 'for four years') for a relationship, membership, or repeated activity, extract it as a fact even if embedded in a conversational or rhetorical turn.
content: During extraction, treat explicit time-span phrases (e.g., 'for X years', 'for X months') as factual details whenever they qualify a relationship, group membership, role, or repeated activity; produce a candidate (e.g., as an event or relationship) that records both the relationship/activity and its duration.
Do not skip extraction solely because the statement appears inside a rhetorical question or a casual conversational follow-up; the factual content still belongs in long-term memory.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: the extractor skipped an explicit duration fact ('four years') tied to a relationship because it appeared in a rhetorical turn. The rule abstracts that failure into a general extraction requirement: always capture time-span phrases qualifying a relationship, membership, or repeated activity, no matter the conversational framing. Applies to any future message stating how long such a connection lasted.

payload.name: Duplicate-skip requires existing memory match
payload.description: When a construction decision considers SKIP because a candidate seems duplicated, verify that the existing memory pool actually contains a memory covering the candidate's content; empty or unrelated pools do not justify SKIP.
content: Before choosing SKIP with reason 'duplicate already represented,' confirm that a retrieved existing memory actually covers the candidate's subject, predicate, and time window.
If the existing-memory pool is empty or contains no related memory, the candidate is new: ADD it instead of skipping.
Only SKIP when a concrete existing memory version is displayed or referenced in the retrieval pool; do not assume duplication from the candidate's wording alone.

candidates.solves: Construction decisions sometimes skip a candidate as a duplicate without confirming that the memory pool actually contains a covering memory, silently dropping facts. This skill forces a verification step before any duplicate-based SKIP and applies to all future construction decisions where the pool appears empty or unrelated.

payload.name: Verify memory coverage before skipping a candidate
payload.description: When deciding whether to SKIP a memory candidate as already covered or duplicated during construction, use this to require concrete evidence of an existing memory.
content: Before SKIPping an ADD candidate because the fact is 'already included', confirm that a memory containing that exact fact exists in the retrieved existing-memory pool or in a memory committed earlier in the same batch. If no such memory exists, issue ADD instead.

Every SKIP must reference a concrete memory ID or version whose stored content actually covers the candidate's content. Do not use the reason 'already included in the updated memory' when no matching update or memory exists.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes SKIP new-memory candidates with the reason 'information already included in the updated memory' even when no memory pool or committed change actually contains that fact, permanently losing the fact. This rule applies to any ADD/MERGE decision where the candidate would be the only stored record of the information; it does not apply when an identical memory version is visible in the retrieved pool or previously committed in the same batch.

payload.name: Verify existing-memory match before duplicate SKIP
payload.description: When deciding to SKIP a candidate during CRUD because information is already represented, first confirm the matching memory actually exists in the retrieved pool.
content: During CRUD, before applying SKIP with the reason 'information already represented', require an actual matching memory in the retrieved existing-memory pool; if no relevant memory is present, the candidate is new and should be ADDed or MERGEd instead.
Do not assume a fact is already represented merely because earlier messages discussed a similar topic; absence of a retrieved memory makes the SKIP justification invalid.

candidates.solves: During construction CRUD, a valid new fact candidate is sometimes skipped with the justification that the information is already represented even though no matching memory exists in the retrieved pool, causing a true fact to be lost. This rule applies whenever a SKIP decision is considered and requires grounding any 'already represented' claim in an explicit existing-memory match before skipping.

payload.name: Preserve-new-facts-when-overlapping-existing-memory
payload.description: When a construction candidate overlaps an existing memory topic, check whether it adds a fact (feeling, state, preference, relationship) not already stored; if so, update or add instead of skipping.
content: During extraction or CRUD decision, before skipping or merging a candidate because it seems to duplicate an existing memory, compare facts field-by-field. If the candidate contains a new predicate (emotional response, preference, state, relationship quality) absent from the target memory, do not skip: create a new memory or enrich the existing one with the added fact.

When updating an existing memory, preserve the original content and append/merge the new fact; do not let partial-topic overlap (e.g., same entity or ownership) justify discarding the new information.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes skip or overwrite candidates that share an entity with an existing memory but contain distinct new facts, such as feelings, preferences, or relationship quality, losing evidence needed later. This rule teaches comparing candidate facts against the stored memory and retaining any new fact via add or enrichment.

payload.name: Confirm duplicate against existing memory before SKIP
payload.description: When deciding to SKIP a construction candidate as a duplicate, first verify that the retrieved existing-memory pool actually contains a memory fully representing the candidate's fact; if not, do not skip.
content: Before marking a candidate as SKIP because it is a duplicate, confirm that an existing memory in the pool fully represents the same subject, fact/event, and details; absence of such a memory means the candidate is not a duplicate.
If the memory pool is empty or no retrieved memory contains equivalent information, do not SKIP; instead ADD the candidate as a new memory or UPDATE/MERGE with a relevant existing memory.
Never skip a candidate merely because the fact seems implied by conversation history; the fact must already exist as a memory version in the pool.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes skip a correctly extracted candidate as a duplicate even when no existing memory actually contains the fact, causing the information to be lost from memory. This rule requires duplicate SKIP decisions to be grounded in a retrieved memory that fully represents the candidate's content, and applies to any decision stage where a candidate is judged against an empty or sparse memory pool.

payload.name: Distinct-instance overlap check
payload.description: When evaluating a memory candidate during construction, apply before deciding to SKIP it as overlapping; if the candidate reports a new specific instance of a recurring activity or object that is distinct from existing memories of the same category, ADD it as a separate memory instead of discarding it.
content: During candidate evaluation, only SKIP or merge a candidate as overlapping if it refers to the same specific fact, entity, or instance already captured (e.g., same event, same object, same project).

If a candidate reports a new instance of a recurring activity or object (e.g., starting a new book, taking a new class, adopting another pet) that differs from previously stored instances, preserve it as a separate memory via ADD; UPDATE only when the candidate extends that same instance.
Treat category-level similarity (e.g., both are writing projects, both are classes) as insufficient reason to drop a candidate; distinct instances are durable facts that must be retained.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is a construction decision that skipped a candidate about starting a book as overlapping with an existing screenplay memory, conflating distinct writing projects. The failure mechanism is treating same-category items as duplicates. This rule applies to any future session where a new concrete instance (book, course, project, pet, etc.) belongs to an already-memorized category but is a separate fact to be stored.

payload.name: Verify-duplicate-before-skip
payload.description: When a construction candidate seems already covered by existing memory, before skipping it as a duplicate, confirm that an existing memory actually contains the same fact or its semantic equivalent; otherwise ADD or MERGE.
content: During CRUD decisions, only SKIP a candidate as a duplicate when the retrieved memory pool contains a memory with the same fact or its semantic equivalent.

If a candidate adds a new specific item, instance, or detail that no existing memory states exactly or equivalently, do not SKIP it; ADD it as a new memory or MERGE it into the closest related memory.

candidates.solves: During construction CRUD, a candidate was skipped as a duplicate although no existing memory contained that fact, permanently losing new specific information (e.g., a newly tried yoga pose). The abstract failure is treating a semantically related or topically similar memory as covering a distinct specific fact. This rule applies to any future session where candidates with new details are at risk of being discarded during deduplication.

payload.name: Verify-Memory-Coverage-Before-Skip
payload.description: When deciding whether to SKIP a construction candidate because it is 'already fully represented in existing memory', first verify that the retrieved existing-memory pool actually contains a memory covering the candidate's claims. Apply before finalizing any SKIP decision.
content: During the CRUD decision stage, never SKIP a candidate with the reason 'already fully represented in existing memory' unless a memory in the retrieved pool explicitly covers the candidate's claims (same subject, event or state, and key details).
If the retrieved pool contains no such covering memory, the candidate is not yet stored; choose ADD (or MERGE only when the candidate extends an existing memory) instead of SKIP.
A memory that is thematically similar or mentions the same subject but omits the specific claim does not count as coverage.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure was a SKIP where no existing memory covered the candidate, causing a supported fact to never be persisted. The reusable mechanism is unverified SKIPs based on an assumption of coverage. This rule applies to any future construction session where a candidate is skipped as 'already represented' but the retrieved memory pool lacks an equivalent memory; it does not apply when the pool genuinely contains a covering memory, where SKIP remains correct.

payload.name: Verify existing memory before redundant SKIP
payload.description: When deciding to SKIP a candidate because it duplicates an existing memory, first confirm that the existing memory is actually present in the retrieved memory pool and covers the candidate fact.
content: Before applying SKIP due to redundancy, verify that the referenced existing memory is present in the retrieved memory pool and semantically covers the candidate's key fact.
If no such memory exists in the retrieved pool, do not SKIP; ADD the candidate as a new memory (or apply the appropriate UPDATE/MERGE).
Do not assume redundancy from conversation context, earlier turns, or memories not actually retrieved in the current decision stage.

candidates.solves: During construction decision, candidates may be SKIPped as redundant based on an assumed existing memory even when the retrieved memory pool contains no such memory. This rule applies whenever a SKIP reason cites coverage by an existing memory: require that memory to be present in the retrieved pool and to actually cover the candidate fact before skipping.

payload.name: Verify duplicate before SKIP in construction decisions
payload.description: When a construction candidate is being SKIPped as a duplicate or already fully represented, apply this rule to verify actual overlap with an existing memory before skipping.
content: Before applying SKIP for 'duplicate or already fully represented', verify that an existing memory in the retrieved pool actually covers the candidate's fact; absence of a matching memory means the candidate is new and must be added.
Do not infer duplication from same-subject but different-aspect memories; only skip if the existing memory substantively represents the candidate's fact.

candidates.solves: Future problem pattern: a valid extraction candidate is skipped as a duplicate even though the retrieved memory pool contains no memory covering that fact, leaving the memory missing. The skill corrects this by requiring verification of actual overlap before SKIP; it does not apply when a genuine duplicate memory exists.

payload.name: Extract coping and comfort preferences
payload.description: When a user mentions activities, pets, or items that help them cope, distract, or comfort them during hard times, extract them as preference/relationship memories.
content: During extraction, if a message explicitly states that an activity, pet, item, or person helps the user cope, stay distracted, or feel better during tough times, create a candidate memory for each mentioned helper.
Record the helper in a compact memory: use preference for activities or items, relationship (pet) for animals, and include the role ('helps during tough times') in the content.
Attach the source message as evidence and keep the memory durable and source-linked per normal conventions.

candidates.solves: The Construction Agent failed to extract any candidate from a message where the user explicitly stated that video games and a pet helped them stay distracted during tough times. The abstract mechanism is that explicit statements of coping or comforting activities are often missed because they are phrased as casual support ('really helps', 'nice distraction') rather than direct 'I like X'. This rule applies whenever a future message explicitly mentions things that help the user during difficult periods, so these facts are not lost.

payload.name: Extract-Explicit-Affection-Statements
payload.description: Apply during extraction when a speaker explicitly states affection or emotional evaluation toward a person, pet, or object while recounting an experience; create a durable preference or relationship memory even if the event was already covered.
content: During extraction, if a message contains an explicit statement of the speaker's affection or emotional evaluation about a person, pet, or object (e.g., 'It showed how much I love her'), create a candidate preference or relationship memory for that sentiment.
Do not skip a message solely because its event details were already captured; the evaluative statement is a separate durable fact.
Link the new memory to the source message and, when present, to the related event memory.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is an extraction miss: a message containing the speaker's explicit affection statement about her pet, embedded in a past-event narrative, produced no candidate, so the sentiment was never persisted. The abstract mechanism is treating personal evaluative statements as non-memory-worthy narration. This rule applies to future sessions where a user explicitly expresses an emotional evaluation about a person, pet, or object; those expressions should be extracted as durable preference/relationship memories.

payload.name: Preserve explicit evaluative descriptors in memories
payload.description: When extracting or updating a memory from a message where a speaker explicitly evaluates a person, event, or object with a descriptive adjective, retain that exact descriptor in the memory content.
content: During extraction, if the source message contains an explicit evaluative adjective describing a person, event, or object (e.g., 'amazing', 'wonderful', 'terrible'), include that term verbatim in the candidate content instead of only paraphrasing the sentiment.

During UPDATE/MERGE enrichment of an existing memory, carry forward any previously captured explicit descriptors and add any new explicit descriptors from the new evidence; do not replace specific evaluative wording with a general sentiment summary.
Ensure the memory content preserves the speaker's exact descriptive term so future questions about how something was described can be answered from memory alone.

candidates.solves: When a speaker explicitly evaluates a subject with a specific adjective, extraction candidates tend to paraphrase the sentiment (e.g., 'excitement') and drop the exact descriptor (e.g., 'amazing'), making later factual questions about the description unanswerable from memory. This rule applies to any future construction step where a message contains an explicit evaluative phrase about a person, object, or event, and ensures the descriptor is preserved verbatim.

payload.name: Capture all explicitly stated emotions during extraction
payload.description: When a message explicitly expresses multiple or contrasting feelings about the same subject (e.g., 'discouraged but determined'), include every distinct emotion in the extracted memory instead of only one.
content: During extraction, if a message explicitly names more than one emotion or feeling about the same subject, represent each distinct emotion in the memory content (e.g., both 'discouraged' and 'determined').
When updating an existing memory, preserve previously captured emotions unless the new evidence explicitly replaces them.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: an extraction candidate captured only the 'determined' feeling from 'A bit discouraged but I'm determined,' dropping the discouragement. The failure mechanism is selective capture when a message explicitly states multiple emotions about the same subject. A rule requiring all explicitly expressed emotions to be preserved generalizes across any mixed/contrasting feeling, preventing incomplete memory that later fails questions about the omitted emotion.

payload.name: Preserve explicit activities in event memory extraction
payload.description: When extracting an event memory from a message where the speaker describes something they did or enjoyed, include the specific activities/actions they mention, not only emotions or associated recollections.
content: During extraction of event memories, capture the explicit activities or actions the speaker performed or enjoyed (e.g., danced, hiked, cooked) as part of the candidate content.
Do not let emotional descriptors (e.g., freeing, magical) or tangential memories replace the concrete activity facts; include both when the message contains them.

candidates.solves: During extraction, event memories were summarized with emotional descriptors and tangential recollections but omitted the explicit activity the speaker said they enjoyed, so later questions about what the person did could not be answered. The rule applies to any message that describes an event the speaker participated in: preserve the concrete action phrases (e.g., dancing, hiking) as event facts alongside feelings, because those verb phrases are the retrievable content future questions target.

payload.name: Include explicitly stated feelings in extraction candidates
payload.description: During extraction, when a user explicitly names an emotion or feeling about an experience or memory, preserve that feeling in the memory content; do not keep only activities or factual details.
content: When extracting a memory from a message that explicitly states a feeling or emotion (e.g., 'I feel peace and gratitude', 'it makes me happy'), include the named feeling in the candidate content together with the event or subject it refers to.

If the experience or event is already represented in memory but the message adds a new explicit feeling about it, still produce an extraction candidate that captures the new feeling rather than skipping it as fully duplicated.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates sometimes record only activities or facts from a user's recollection and omit the explicitly stated emotional response (e.g., 'I feel peace and gratitude'), so the memory cannot later answer questions about feelings. This Skill applies whenever a future message contains an explicit feeling/emotion tied to an experience, place, or memory; it does not apply to inferring emotions the user never stated.

payload.name: Preserve stated hopes and impact goals in memories
payload.description: When extracting or enriching a memory from a user statement that expresses a hope, goal, or desired impact for an activity or creative work, capture that aspiration alongside any personal or emotional benefits.
content: During extraction, if a user explicitly states a hope, goal, or desired impact for an activity (e.g., sharing it with others or making a difference), record that aspiration as a durable fact in the memory candidate, not only the activity's personal or emotional benefits.

During UPDATE/MERGE enrichment of an existing activity-related memory, check the new message for an externally-oriented purpose or audience; if present, add it while preserving previously remembered intrinsic benefits.
Treat intrinsic emotional value (e.g., escape, healing, expression) and externally-oriented intent (e.g., sharing, impact) as distinct facts; do not let one replace or absorb the other.

candidates.solves: When a user explicitly states a hope, goal, or desired impact for an activity (e.g., sharing creative work or making a difference), extraction often records only intrinsic emotional benefits and drops the external aspiration. This makes later questions about intended impact unanswerable from memory. The rule applies whenever a statement attaches purpose, audience, or desired effect to an activity during candidate extraction or memory enrichment, regardless of the activity or person.

payload.name: Extract explicit pet activity statements
payload.description: When a message explicitly mentions the user doing an activity with their pet, use this Skill during extraction to create a memory candidate.
content: During extraction, if a message explicitly states that the speaker does an activity with their pet (e.g., hiking, walking), create an extraction candidate for that activity.
Record the candidate as a 'state' or 'event' memory linked to the pet relationship; do not discard it because the pet is named or the activity seems casual.
Only extract what is explicitly stated; do not generalize to other activities or pets.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction skips explicit user statements about activities they do with their pets, so later questions about those activities are unsupported. Add an extraction candidate whenever a pet activity (walking, hiking, etc.) is explicitly mentioned, recording it as a state or event tied to the pet relationship. Applies to any stated pet-activity fact; does not apply to inferring unstated activities.

payload.name: PreserveExplicitProcessDescriptions
payload.description: When a message contains an explicit description of the process, manner, or approach used for an action or creation, use this skill during extraction to preserve that description as a distinct memory fact.
content: During candidate extraction, if the speaker explicitly describes the process, manner, or approach of performing an action or creating something, preserve that explicit description as a separate memory fact, even when the message also contains emotional reactions or descriptions of the outcome.

Do not fold explicit process/manner statements into a summary of emotions or results. Keep them as distinct facts so the memory can answer future questions about how the speaker described the process.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause was extraction producing a summary of emotions and outcomes while omitting the speaker's explicit description of the creative process, leaving the memory unable to answer 'how was the process described'. The rule abstracts this by requiring explicit process/manner statements to be extracted as distinct facts; it applies to any future session where a speaker explicitly describes how an action or creation was performed, across any topic.

payload.name: Preserve explicit influence concepts during extraction
payload.description: When a user states how a book, film, or other work influenced their perspective, use the specific concepts they explicitly named in the extracted or enriched memory.
content: When extracting a memory from a statement about how a book, film, or other work changed the user's perspective, preserve the specific concepts they explicitly named (e.g., 'searching for personal legends') in the candidate content.
Do not reduce explicitly named effects to a generic summary (e.g., 'motivated to pursue dreams') that drops their terminology; keep both when both are stated.
During UPDATE or merge enrichment, append new details without removing or replacing previously stored named concepts.

candidates.solves: Extraction often paraphrases a user's statement about a book's influence into generic wording, dropping explicitly named concepts (e.g., 'personal legends'), so later questions about that influence cannot be answered. The rule—retain explicitly named effects during extraction and enrichment—applies to any book, film, or experience where the user names specific concepts or goals; not applicable when no such concept is named.

payload.name: Preserve explicit outcomes in extracted memories
payload.description: When extracting memory content from evidence that states a concrete outcome, achievement, or goal someone helped others reach, include that explicit outcome in the candidate instead of a broader paraphrase.
content: During extraction, if the source explicitly states a result, achievement, or goal (e.g., 'reach their goals', 'achieve X'), preserve that exact outcome in the candidate content; do not replace it with a broader phrase like 'growth and development' that omits it.
When updating or merging existing memories, verify that any explicit outcome or achievement mentioned in the source is retained in the new version; do not let summarization strip answerable details.

candidates.solves: During extraction, paraphrasing evidence can drop explicit outcome claims (e.g., 'develop and reach their goals' became 'growth and development'), leaving later QA unsupported. The reusable mechanism is losing concrete results, achievements, or goals while summarizing. This rule applies to any future construction task where source text names a specific outcome a person helped others reach; it ensures memory content preserves answerable claims explicitly.

payload.name: Separate challenge and achievement memories
payload.description: When a statement contains both a struggle/challenge and a positive outcome or achievement about the same subject, create separate memories for the two facts during construction.
content: During extraction and decision, when a message describes both a difficulty/challenge and a positive result or achievement for the same subject, split them into two distinct event memories rather than one combined memory.
Ensure each memory content preserves its own valence: keep the challenge description and the achievement/outcome description on separate memories so both facts are independently retrievable.

candidates.solves: A construction decision merged a stated difficulty ('tough time with English lit') and a positive outcome ('analysis went ok') into a single memory that encoded only the challenge, hiding the achievement from later retrieval. The abstract failure is conflating opposite-valence facts about the same subject in one memory. This rule applies whenever a message contains both a struggle/challenge and a success/achievement, requiring separate durable memories per fact so each remains retrievable.

payload.name: Preserve Distinct Concrete Functions in Extraction
payload.description: When extracting memory from a message in which a person says a tool, device, or service has several specific functions, use this to preserve each concrete function explicitly instead of collapsing them into a generic benefit.
content: During extraction, if the source states multiple distinct concrete functions or effects of an object, preserve each as its own explicit clause or candidate; do not replace any specific function with a broader generalization such as 'stay motivated'.

When a directly stated fact (e.g., 'serves as a constant reminder to keep going') is clear, include its specific wording or a faithful close paraphrase in the candidate content, even if another clause summarizes the overall purpose.

candidates.solves: When a user states that a tool, device, or service provides several distinct concrete functions (e.g., tracks progress, serves as a reminder, gives alerts), extraction candidates sometimes replace one specific function with a broader generalization, losing answerable facts. The fix is to preserve each explicit concrete function rather than collapsing it into an umbrella term like motivation.

payload.name: CaptureExplicitStatedMotivations
payload.description: During extraction, when a message pairs an action or routine with an explicit stated reason, value, or motivation (e.g., 'because', 'important to me'), capture that motivation as a preference or state memory instead of recording only the activity.
content: During extraction, when a speaker states an action and explicitly explains why (using phrases like 'because', 'so that', 'is important to me', 'to help me'), extract the stated reason as a preference or state memory, and keep the activity fact in the same candidate or a linked memory.

Do not let an activity-only candidate (e.g., 'takes cats for runs every morning') substitute for the explicit motivation; both the behavior and its stated rationale are durable facts for future why-questions.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: extraction captured an activity but dropped the explicitly stated motivation, so future why-questions lack evidence. Mechanism: an action paired with a stated reason yields two durable facts; omitting the reason loses a preference claim. Applies whenever a user explains why they do a habit, routine, or choice; not applicable when no reason is given or the motivation is only inferred.

payload.name: Extract concrete events alongside preferences
payload.description: Use when a message states a concrete past action (e.g., cooking a meal) and the same or a following message identifies it; extract the action as an event memory even if the message also contains an attitude.
content: During extraction, if a message states that the subject performed a concrete action (e.g., cooked a meal, made a dish), create a separate 'event' candidate for that action even when the message also expresses an attitude or preference about it; do not let the attitude candidate replace the event.

When a subsequent message from another participant identifies or specifies that action (e.g., names the dish), extract the concrete event from that message if not already captured, or use the identification to confirm and enrich the event candidate.

candidates.solves: Extraction missed a concrete event (cooking a slow cooker meal) because the utterance also contained a preference, and the partner's identifying reply was ignored.
