The rule forces separate event extraction for concrete actions stated in a message and treats a follow-up identification as evidence, preventing future questions about what the person did from being unanswerable.

payload.name: Preserve explicitly stated emotions during memory extraction
payload.description: Use during memory extraction or consolidation when a user explicitly names multiple feelings or emotional states in evidence; preserve each one verbatim without substituting similar emotions.
content: When generating an extraction candidate or condensing several messages into one memory, list every emotion or feeling term the user explicitly stated; do not drop any.

If a user names a specific feeling such as freedom, joy, fear, or hope, do not replace it with a nearby concept that changes the meaning (e.g., inspiration for freedom); the memory must remain faithful to the stated emotion.
Before ADD/UPDATE, verify each explicitly named emotion in the source messages appears in the candidate or updated content.

candidates.solves: Memory extraction sometimes condenses user statements and loses or substitutes explicitly named emotions, producing memories that contradict the evidence. A reusable rule is to preserve every emotion term the user states verbatim during extraction and consolidation, and to check this before ADD/UPDATE. This applies whenever future sessions contain user self-reports of feelings across any topic, and does not apply to inferred emotions or non-emotional facts.

payload.name: CaptureExplicitlyNamedEmotions
payload.description: When a message explicitly names emotions or feelings, record each named emotion during extraction and add newly named emotions during updates.
content: During extraction, if a message contains explicitly named emotions (e.g., relief, excitement, anxiety, worry, hope), include each named emotion in the memory content instead of summarizing as 'mixed emotions' or omitting them.
During updates, when a later message names additional emotions about the same subject, merge those new names into the existing memory rather than replacing them with a vague phrase.

candidates.solves: When users explicitly name emotions about an event or situation, extraction often paraphrases them as 'mixed emotions' or omits them, causing memory gaps that later answers cannot fill. This skill applies to any future message where the speaker states concrete feelings; it does not apply when emotions must be inferred from behavior or context rather than named.

payload.name: Preserve explicit place-feeling links in extraction
payload.description: When a user explicitly states that a specific place or spot gives them a feeling (peace, comfort, joy, calm), preserve that exact place-feeling link during extraction instead of folding it into a broader activity summary.
content: During extraction, when the speaker explicitly names a specific place/spot and states the feeling it gives them (e.g., 'gives me peace', 'makes me feel calm'), record that place-feeling link as its own state or event candidate, preserving the location name and feeling verbatim.

Do not replace the place-feeling link with a broader summary of the activity done there; if an activity memory already exists for that context, the place-feeling link should still be recorded explicitly (as a new candidate or an UPDATE enrichment to the existing memory).
During CRUD, if the exact place-feeling link already exists, SKIP; if the place is present but the feeling is missing (or vice versa), enrich the existing memory with the missing half.

candidates.solves: Extraction dropped an explicit place-feeling statement ('spot by the window gives me peace') by folding it into a broader activity summary. This skill applies whenever a speaker explicitly names a place/spot and links it to an emotional state; the rule keeps that place-feeling attribution as a durable memory. It does not apply to implied emotions or summaries lacking an explicit place-feeling link.

payload.name: Extract inspiration-source memories from causal statements
payload.description: When a user states that a place, experience, or observation 'sparked', 'inspired', or 'gave ideas for' their creative work or project, extract a memory connecting that source to the work.
content: During extraction, always treat explicit causal statements like 'X sparked ideas for my Y' or 'X inspired my Y' as candidates for a memory recording that Y was inspired by X.
Do not skip these when the source is described in a preceding sentence or when the word 'inspired' is not used literally. Capture the source and the work it inspired.

candidates.solves: The extraction stage produced no candidate from a message in which the user explicitly said a place's history 'sparked ideas for my next script', so the inspiration fact was lost. The underlying failure is that causal inspiration statements were not recognized as memory-worthy facts. This skill applies to any future message where a user links a source (place, event, experience) to their creative work using causal phrasing, ensuring the connection is captured as a memory.

payload.name: Preserve explicit qualifiers during candidate extraction
payload.description: During candidate extraction, when a speaker qualifies a feeling or memory with an explicit adjective phrase (e.g., 'peaceful moments'), preserve that qualifier exactly instead of paraphrasing it to a generic term.
content: During candidate extraction, when a speaker expresses a sentiment about an activity or experience and attaches an explicit qualifier (e.g., 'peaceful moments'), copy that qualifier into the candidate instead of replacing it with a generic noun.

Before finalizing an extracted candidate, re-check the raw message for salient felt descriptors; if the paraphrase dropped any, revise the candidate so the durable memory keeps the speaker's exact qualitative detail.

candidates.solves: Cause: extraction paraphrased away the speaker's explicit qualifier, so the memory missed the detail a later question targeted. The mechanism is lossy generalization of felt descriptors during candidate extraction and recurs across any qualified experience. Use the rule whenever a speaker qualifies a sentiment with a descriptive phrase; it does not apply to CRUD operations or unqualified neutral context.

payload.name: PreserveSpecificWorkTypeInMemoryExtraction
payload.description: When extracting a memory about completing or discussing a creative or professional work, if the speaker names a specific artifact type (screenplay, novel, song, etc.), use that type in the memory content instead of a generic label like 'creative project'.
content: During extraction, when a user mentions completing a creative or professional work, capture the exact artifact type they name (e.g., screenplay, novel, song, painting, script) in the memory content; never downgrade it to generic terms like 'creative project'.

Before adding such an event memory, check existing memories of the same subject for prior instances of that artifact type, and phrase the new memory so the type is explicit and countable, enabling future aggregation.
If the statement explicitly confirms an ordinal instance ('my third one', 'another one'), include both the category and the ordinal evidence in the content when inferable from conversational context.

candidates.solves: This addresses extraction failures where a concrete work-type label is replaced by a generic category term, destroying the ability to count or aggregate works of that type (e.g., 'third screenplay' becomes 'creative project'). Applicable to any future construction pass where a user confirms or describes completing instances of a named creative or professional artifact; not applicable to purely emotional or preference summaries.

payload.name: Preserve specific relational meaning in extraction
payload.description: When a user says an activity is comforting or meaningful because it makes them feel connected to, or still experiencing it with, another person, preserve that specific relational claim and its emotional framing when extracting or updating memory candidates.
content: During extraction, if the message includes an explicit relational or experiential explanation (e.g., "it's like we're still experiencing it together", "it comforts me because I go with her"), include the specific activity, the person it relates to, and the claimed emotional benefit in the candidate content.

Do not replace the specific shared-experience claim with a generic statement about emotions or interests; the memory must record the stated reason the activity is meaningful, including "comforting" when said.
Before approving an UPDATE or enrichment, check that the proposed new version retains this specific relational and emotional content; if the candidate omitted it, revise or reject the candidate.

candidates.solves: When a user explains an activity as comforting or meaningful because it connects them to another person (e.g., 'it's like we're still experiencing it together'), extraction candidates often drop that specific relational reason, leaving memories unable to answer questions about it. This rule applies during extraction or before UPDATE to preserve the activity, the person, and the stated comfort.

payload.name: Extract explicit feelings about activities
payload.description: When the user explicitly states feelings or emotional reactions to an activity or experience, extract them as a state or preference memory.
content: During extraction, when the speaker explicitly reports their own feelings or evaluation of an activity/experience (e.g., 'super exciting', 'free-feeling'), create a candidate memory (state or preference) linking the activity to that feeling. Include the explicit feeling terms; do not skip brief or conversational statements.

candidates.solves: The extraction stage generated no candidate from an explicit first-person statement about how the user feels during an activity, so the fact was never stored. The failure mechanism is failing to recognize subjective affective self-reports as durable memory content. A rule to extract such statements applies to any future session where a user describes their feelings or evaluations of an activity.

payload.name: Capture explicit reasons for actions in event extraction
payload.description: During memory extraction, when a message states what inspired or motivated an action, include that reason in the event memory instead of only recording the action.
content: During extraction, if a user explicitly states why they did something (e.g., what inspired or motivated the action), record that reason as part of the event memory or as a linked memory; do not drop it in favor of the action alone.
If the message contains both the action and its stated cause, combine them in one compact event memory so the motivation remains evidence-bound and retrievable.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: an extraction candidate recorded only the action and omitted the explicitly stated inspiration, leaving the memory incomplete. The reusable rule is that any stated reason, motivation, or inspiration for an action is a durable fact and should be captured with the action in the event memory. Applies to any future message where a speaker explains why they did something.

payload.name: Extract activity origin stories separately from preferences
payload.description: When a user explicitly explains how or why they started an activity, hobby, or interest, extract the initiating cause as its own memory instead of only recording the ongoing preference or state.
content: During extraction, if a message contains an explicit origin statement for an activity, hobby, or interest (e.g., 'X got me into it', 'a friend gave me ... and it inspired me', 'it all started when ...'), create a separate event or relationship memory capturing the initiator, the trigger (gift, advice, inspiration), and the onset time.
Do not merge the origin story into an existing general preference or current-state memory; keep the causal how-it-started fact distinct so it remains retrievable.
Only extract an origin when the speaker explicitly states one; do not infer initiators or causes from mere enjoyment or duration of the activity.

candidates.solves: Extraction sometimes drops the origin story when a user explains how they got into an activity, keeping only the resulting preference or current state. This happens when adjacent turns are merged into one preference memory and causal phrases like 'got me into it' or 'it all started when' are overlooked. A general rule to separately capture the initiating event and its trigger applies to any future conversation where someone states who or what started them on a hobby, interest, or behavior.

payload.name: Extract Hobbies From Emotional Context
payload.description: When a message contains an explicit hobby, interest, or passion statement within emotional or nostalgic context, create a profile/preference candidate during extraction.
content: During extraction, if a message explicitly names a person's hobby, interest, or passion (e.g., 'X was one of her hobbies', 'Y was her great passion'), create a profile or preference candidate for it even when the surrounding text is grief-focused, nostalgic, or otherwise emotional.
Do not let an emotional summary candidate (e.g., about grieving or comfort) replace the factual hobby statement; keep hobbies as durable, queryable profile/preference memories.
If several distinct hobbies appear across messages, ensure each becomes part of an accumulated profile/preference memory so later questions about hobbies can be answered from memory.

candidates.solves: Construction passes sometimes collapse explicit hobby or passion statements into an emotional event/state memory and lose the fact. The reusable rule is that any explicit statement of a person's hobby, interest, or passion—even inside grief, nostalgia, or other affective narrative—must be extracted as a durable profile or preference memory. This applies to any future session where a user mentions a person's hobbies or passions amid emotional context.

payload.name: Preserve benefit clauses in interest extraction
payload.description: When a user describes an activity or interest with explicit effects, benefits, or purposes (e.g., escape, imagination, stress relief, creativity), keep those attributes in the extracted candidate.
content: During candidate extraction, when a profile/interest statement includes explicit benefits, effects, or purposes (e.g., helps me escape, stimulates my imagination, expresses my creativity), preserve those clauses as distinct attributes in the candidate rather than summarizing only the liking or enjoyment.

Treat stated effects/purposes as part of the durable fact: if the message says an activity does X for the person, record that the activity 'is a way to X' or 'helps with X' so later queries about that effect remain answerable.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is an extraction that dropped a stated benefit clause (e.g., 'great escape', 'gets my imagination going') and kept only the enjoyment clause, leaving the memory unable to answer which activity produces that effect. The abstract mechanism is summarizing an interest statement without carrying its effect/purpose attributes. Future inputs sharing this pattern—where a speaker states why an activity matters—need the extraction rule above. It does not apply to statements without explicit reasons or to purely factual event extraction.

payload.name: Extract-Explicit-Emotional-Reactions
payload.description: When extracting memories from a message, include explicit emotional reactions and evaluations even if the message also contains plans, goals, or factual updates.
content: During extraction, treat explicit emotional reactions and evaluations (e.g., 'thrilled', 'rewarding') as memory-worthy facts independent of any plans or actions in the same message.
If a message mixes intentions with feelings, preserve the feeling in its own candidate or as an additional enrichment; do not let the plan-focused content replace the emotional fact.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates often capture plans and actions while omitting explicitly stated emotional reactions, causing those feelings to be missing from memory. This rule applies whenever a message mixes goals with stated emotions; it preserves explicit affective statements without requiring inference of unstated feelings.

payload.name: Preserve evaluated activity in memories
payload.description: When a speaker evaluates an action or experience with a feeling word (freeing, fun, magical, etc.), include the specific activity being evaluated in the extracted memory, not just the evaluation.
content: When extracting a memory from a statement containing an evaluative expression (e.g., 'It was so freeing to dance and bop around'), store the concrete activity that is evaluated, not only the emotion or general description.
Keep the evaluation and its object together in the memory content so that both the feeling and its referent are retrievable.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes stores only the evaluative summary of an experience (e.g., 'it was freeing') and drops the concrete activity that the evaluation refers to. This rule addresses future messages where a feeling or quality is attached to a specific action or event; it requires the extractor to preserve the object of the evaluation so later questions about 'what' can be answered.

payload.name: Extract explicit evaluative statements about activities
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly evaluates an activity, hobby, or experience with an adjective or feeling word (e.g., magical, fun, exciting) in any message, extract that as a preference or state candidate, even if the message also contains encouragement or directives.
content: During candidate extraction, scan every message for explicit evaluative clauses about activities, experiences, or objects (e.g., 'it is magical', 'it feels exciting'). If present, create a preference or state candidate attributed to the speaker.
Do not skip a candidate just because the same message also contains encouragement, advice, or a directive. The evaluative clause is independently memory-worthy.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure was that no extraction candidate was generated from a message where Gina explicitly described dance as magical, so the fact was never stored. The abstract mechanism is an extraction gap for explicit evaluative statements embedded in non-factual or encouraging messages. This rule applies to any future session where a speaker makes a clear value judgment about an activity, regardless of topic.

payload.name: Extract origin alongside preference or state
payload.description: When a user mentions a hobby, interest, preference, or life state and also states how it started or what caused it, apply during extraction.
content: During extraction, if a message contains both a current preference/state and the reason or origin behind it, do not extract only the current state. Also capture the origin as a separate durable memory (e.g., event or relationship) or include it in the same candidate when it is a single coherent fact.
Before finalizing a candidate, check whether the source message answers 'how did this begin?' or 'what caused this?'; if yes, ensure that answer is represented in the extracted candidate set.

candidates.solves: During extraction, a preference or state is often summarized without the origin that explains how it began. This failure is reusable because future questions commonly ask how or why someone acquired a hobby, interest, role, or preference; the answer is present in the same user message but missing from the extracted candidate. The rule applies whenever a user states both a current interest and its trigger/origin; it does not apply when no origin is mentioned.

payload.name: Preserve-Explicit-Subjective-Evaluations
payload.description: When a message states an event plus an explicit subjective evaluation or feeling about it (e.g., 'it was a huge success', 'I was relieved'), apply during extraction and memory updates to keep the evaluation in memory, not only the concrete event.
content: When a message contains both an event and an explicit subjective evaluation, feeling, or judgment about that event (e.g., 'jogging without pain was a huge success', 'I was thrilled'), extract and store the evaluation as well as the event itself; do not drop it because it is not a concrete action.
Represent the evaluation as its own memory candidate (e.g., an event or state about the speaker's assessment) or fold it into the event memory so the speaker's expressed feeling remains retrievable.
During CRUD, when evaluating extraction candidates or existing memories, do not merge away an explicit evaluation solely because the event it refers to is already recorded.

candidates.solves: Extraction captured only the concrete celebration event and dropped the speaker's explicit evaluation ('a huge success'), leaving later feeling questions unanswerable. The mechanism is omitting subjective evaluations when an event is present. Apply to any message pairing an event with an explicit feeling or judgment (relief, pride, disappointment) so feeling-related questions remain answerable.

payload.name: Preserve object specifics in creation events
payload.description: When extracting or updating event memories about creating, making, producing, or acquiring something, include the specific object noun phrase from the evidence instead of a generic description.
content: During extraction, when evidence states what someone created, made, produced, or acquired (e.g., 'a limited edition line of hoodies'), record the full specific object noun phrase in the memory content; do not replace it with a generic term like 'a line' or 'items'.
When updating or merging such event memories, preserve the object specification and add it if missing; only include specifics directly stated or clearly implied by the source, never invented.

candidates.solves: Extraction may drop the specific object of creation/production verbs, e.g., recording 'made a limited edition line' instead of 'made a limited edition line of hoodies,' losing the key noun that later questions target. This rule preserves concrete object noun phrases from evidence and applies whenever a speaker states what they created, made, produced, or acquired; it does not apply when no specific object is stated.

payload.name: Extract general peace-and-comfort statements
payload.description: When a user says something gives them peace, comfort, or helps them cope during difficult times, extract it as a memory candidate even if phrased generally.
content: During extraction, if the user states that an activity, object, practice, place, or person brings them peace, comfort, or helps them cope during difficult times, create a durable memory candidate. Use profile for recurring sources of comfort and event for time-bound coping episodes.
Do not skip such statements merely because they are phrased as general observations (e.g., 'X gives me peace', 'Y helps me through hard times') rather than explicit preferences or narrated events.
When committing, preserve the source link and resolve relative timing from the message timestamp; avoid merging the extracted comfort source into an unrelated existing memory.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction misses user statements that describe what brings the user peace, comfort, or coping strength during difficult times when those statements are phrased generally rather than as events. This skill ensures such statements are extracted as durable preferences or time-bound events in future sessions whenever a user attributes comfort or coping to a specific activity, object, place, or person; it does not apply to momentary emotional expressions without an attributed source.

payload.name: Extract person-attributed inspiration separately from analogy
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly credits another person's boldness, courage, or other quality as inspiring them, and then relates an analogy or anecdote (nature, hike, story), extract both as distinct durable memories.
content: During extraction, if a message explicitly says a person or their trait/action inspired the speaker, create a durable memory for that attribution, even when the same message continues with an analogy or related anecdote.
Keep the explicit inspiration source and any accompanying analogy as separate candidates; do not let the anecdote absorb the person attribution.
During CRUD, if an existing memory preserves only the anecdote, ADD the missing inspiration-source fact rather than overwriting the anecdote memory to contain both.

candidates.solves: Cause: extraction merged a message with multiple inspiration sources into one event memory, losing the explicit attribution to a person's quality. Rule: preserve each explicitly stated inspiration source as a separate durable memory, so future 'what/who inspires X' questions stay answerable. Applies to any session where a speaker credits a person's trait and also describes a related anecdote; does not apply when no explicit person attribution is present.

payload.name: Extract explicit reactions to past events
payload.description: When a user explicitly describes their emotional reaction or subjective evaluation of a past event or achievement, extract a state/event memory capturing that reaction during candidate extraction.
content: During extraction, treat explicit user statements about how they felt about an event ('It felt crazy', 'I was proud', 'the hard work paid off') as candidate memories of type state or event; do not skip them because they are short or emotional.
Bind the memory to the event it references and use the message timestamp as the occurrence time; keep the memory compact and evidence-bound to the exact wording.
If the same reaction is stated later with more detail, update or merge rather than duplicating; never create a new memory when the user only repeats existing facts without new content.

candidates.solves: The extraction stage sometimes skips a message in which a user explicitly states their reaction to a completed event or achievement (e.g., 'It felt crazy', 'all the hard work paid off'), leaving durable facts unmemoized. This rule makes such explicit subjective evaluations first-class extraction candidates, bound to the event and timestamp, and applies to any future message where the user clearly expresses how they felt about an event. It does not apply to inferring emotions not stated by the user, nor to capturing the answer of the current question.

payload.name: Extract explicit coping-mechanism disclosures
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly states how they deal with doubts, stress, or personal challenges, extract that coping mechanism as a preference or state candidate even if phrased reflectively rather than as a direct preference.
content: During candidate extraction, when a speaker explicitly identifies an activity or habit as their way of dealing with doubts, stress, or other personal challenges, create a preference or state candidate grounded in that message.
Do not require direct preference phrasing ('I like', 'I prefer'); reflective or narrative phrasing such as 'it was my way of dealing with...' is sufficient evidence.
Resolve relative time from the message/session timestamp. Do not apply this rule to speculative, hypothetical, or third-party claims about coping, which lack direct evidence.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that the extraction pass missed an explicit self-disclosure about a coping strategy because it was phrased reflectively rather than as a directly stated preference. This rule applies to future sessions where a speaker directly describes how they handle doubts, stress, or personal challenges. It does not apply to speculative, hypothetical, or third-party claims about coping, which lack direct evidence.

payload.name: Extract self-reported stress-relief and comfort habits
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly mentions their own stress-relief or comfort habits (foods, snacks, activities, places) even in casual or emotional phrasing, extract a preference or event memory for that behavior.
content: During extraction, when a speaker explicitly states how they cope with stress or seek comfort (e.g., foods, snacks, activities, places), create a preference or event candidate for that behavior, even if the utterance also conveys guilt or emotion or is phrased as a rhetorical remark.
Do not extract only the emotional reaction (e.g., guilt) and discard the stated behavior; the concrete habit is the durable fact.
Treat self-disclosed habits as factual preferences of the speaker; do not require positive framing or formal recommendation to record them.

candidates.solves: Extraction missed explicit self-reported coping behavior because emotional framing (guilt) dominated, so no durable habit memory was stored. Future sessions should capture a speaker's own stress-relief foods, activities, or places whenever stated, even casually; not third-party or hypothetical claims.

payload.name: Capture explicit self-reported states
payload.description: When the user explicitly states a current personal condition or challenge (e.g., work stress, motivation), extract it as a `state` memory even from casual asides.
content: During candidate extraction, treat explicit user statements about their current condition or challenge — such as stress, health, workload, or motivation — as extractable `state` facts, even when they appear in brief asides or casual replies.
Do not discard such statements as transient or insubstantial; record them with the message timestamp as the time context.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure was an extraction omission: a user explicitly stated a current personal condition (work stress), but no candidate was extracted, leaving the fact missing from memory. The abstract mechanism is that explicit self-disclosures of current personal state are skipped when they appear in casual asides or brief replies. This skill applies to future sessions whenever a user directly states a current condition, ensuring it is captured as a timestamped state memory.

payload.name: Resolve pronoun antecedents before extracting claims
payload.description: When a statement uses 'they/them' or other pronouns to refer to a previously mentioned entity, use this before extracting a memory to attribute the predicate to the correct subject rather than the speaker.
content: Before extracting a memory candidate, resolve every pronoun in the source message to its nearest plausible antecedent in the same or preceding messages; do not default to the speaker.
When the speaker describes other entities (pets, family, friends) and then uses 'they/them', attribute the predicate to that entity, not the speaker.
If the antecedent is ambiguous or unverifiable, do not guess; either omit the claim or mark it for review instead of assigning a wrong subject.

candidates.solves: The extraction stage misattributed the pronoun 'They' in 'They definitely prefer nice, sunny days in the grass' to the speaker instead of her dogs, producing an incorrect memory. The abstract mechanism is failing to resolve anaphoric pronouns to their antecedents before assigning a memory subject. This rule applies to any future construction pass where a speaker mentions entities (pets, people, objects) and later refers to them with pronouns, ensuring claims are stored under the true referent.

payload.name: Resolve-anaphora-before-memory-extraction
payload.description: When a user statement uses a pronoun or demonstrative (this, it, that) to refer to an object or possession mentioned earlier, resolve the referent from the full conversation before extracting a memory candidate. Use during extraction to avoid mis-attributing the fact.
content: During candidate extraction, if a user statement contains a pronoun or demonstrative (this, it, that, those) referring to an object or possession, resolve it to its antecedent using the full session context before forming the candidate.
Do not assign the nearest noun in the same message automatically; check earlier user or assistant messages for the intended referent, preferring the most recent contextually relevant entity.
Write the extracted candidate with the resolved referent as the subject or object so the expressed fact (reason, motivation, preference) is attributed to the correct entity.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: 'this' was resolved to the wrong object, creating a false candidate and losing the true claim. Mechanism: resolve anaphoric references (this, it, that) from the full conversation before extraction, or facts get mis-attributed. Applies to extraction of reasons, motivations, or attributes about previously mentioned entities; not applicable when referents are unambiguous.

payload.name: Include recipient in recommendation event extraction
payload.description: When a speaker recommends, suggests, or advises something to the conversation partner using second-person pronouns, resolve the addressee from session context and include the recipient in the extracted event memory.
content: During extraction of event memories, when a message contains a recommendation, suggestion, or advice expressed with second-person pronouns (you/your), resolve the addressee from the conversation participants and include the recipient explicitly in the event memory.
Record the event as speaker recommended [object] to [addressee], with the world_start from the message timestamp; do not omit the indirect object.
Add the recipient only when the session context supports it; do not fabricate an addressee when the addressee is ambiguous or unknown.

candidates.solves: Recommendation events are extracted without the recipient, even when the message uses second-person pronouns to the conversation partner. Resolve the addressee from session context and include it, because later questions need the indirect object. Applies to recommendations/suggestions/advice with an identifiable recipient; not to general opinions without a clear addressee.

payload.name: Attribute first-person preferences to the speaker
payload.description: When extracting a preference or opinion expressed in first person, set the memory subject to the speaker, not to other entities mentioned in the message.
content: During extraction, if a message states a preference or opinion in first person (e.g., 'I love', 'my team'), the memory subject must be the speaker of that message.
Do not assign the preference to another participant mentioned in the same or nearby messages unless the message explicitly attributes the opinion to that participant (e.g., 'Tim thinks...').
If the speaker reports someone else's preference (e.g., 'John loves...'), then that named person is the subject; first-person attribution applies only when the speaker talks about themselves.

candidates.solves: Extraction misattributed a first-person preference (John speaking about LeBron) to another participant (Tim), creating a memory about the wrong person and losing the required fact. The reusable rule is to bind first-person statements to the speaker during extraction. This applies whenever a user expresses an opinion or preference about any topic; it does not apply when the message explicitly reports another person's stated preference.

payload.name: Attribute-reported-state-to-referent-subject
payload.description: When a message replies about or reports another person's condition, injury, or state, use the person the statement is about as the memory subject before extracting.
content: Before creating a state, event, or relationship memory, identify the actual person the statement is about; if the speaker is reporting, reassuring, or replying about another person, set subject to that other person, not the speaker.

Resolve pronouns and references by checking the preceding turns; when an utterance attributes a fact or condition to a third party, that third party is the subject even though the statement is spoken by someone else.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction often attributes a state mentioned in a reply to the speaker rather than the person it concerns, causing missing memories. This rule forces subject resolution from referents and preceding context so relayed or reported states are stored under the correct person; applies to any multi-party conversation with conditions, injuries, feelings, or facts reported by another speaker, but not when the speaker is the actual subject.

payload.name: Resolve pronoun referents before writing extraction candidates
payload.description: When a user statement in the session uses a pronoun or demonstrative ('it', 'this', 'that', 'they') to refer to an object, resolve the exact referent from conversation context before writing any memory candidate.
content: Before finalizing an extraction candidate, check whether the source sentence contains a pronoun or demonstrative ('it', 'this', 'that', 'they'); if it does, trace the antecedent through the immediate conversation and set the candidate's object to that resolved referent.

Anchor each candidate in its own message: do not substitute a noun from an earlier or later message merely because it appears in a similar 'I got X…' statement; verify the object against the quoted evidence.
If the referent cannot be resolved confidently, stay close to the literal wording or skip the candidate rather than asserting a different object.

candidates.solves: Cause: the candidate replaced the true referent (bonsai tree) with 'ginger snaps' when the user said 'I got this…'. Abstract mechanism: extraction fails to resolve a pronoun/demonstrative from conversation context and to ground the candidate in its source message. Applies to any future session where a candidate depends on 'it/this/that/they' or similar 'I got X…' statements could be cross-contaminated.

payload.name: Preserve all enumerated items in extraction
payload.description: When a source message explicitly enumerates multiple attributes, themes, preferences, or items about one subject, use this when extracting memory to preserve every listed element in the candidate content.
content: Before creating a memory candidate, scan the source message for explicit enumerations (items separated by commas, 'and', or 'or') attributed to one subject. Every listed item must appear in the extracted content; do not drop or summarize away any enumerated element.

When compressing an enumerated list, preserve each distinct item using concise parallel wording rather than selecting only the most prominent items. Compactness must not come at the cost of omitting explicitly stated facts.

candidates.solves: A construction extraction failed because a candidate summarized an explicit enumeration (e.g., 'sisterhood, love, and reaching for your dreams') and dropped one item, making claims about the dropped item unanswerable. Future inputs that list multiple items, themes, or preferences for one subject risk the same omission. This rule requires extracting every explicitly enumerated element, while not applying to inferred or non-enumerated content.

payload.name: Include all activities when aggregating multi-message events
payload.description: When building one event memory from multiple messages, include every distinct activity or durable fact explicitly mentioned in any source message before finalizing.
content: During extraction, if a candidate summarizes an event described across multiple messages, scan every source message and enumerate each distinct durable fact (activities, locations, outcomes, participants) that is explicitly stated.
Before approving an ADD/MERGE, verify the candidate content contains every enumerated item; do not omit an item because it appears in a later message or seems secondary.
If any explicitly stated item is missing, revise the candidate to include it before writing the memory.

candidates.solves: In construction extraction, an event memory is often aggregated from several messages about the same experience. The diagnosed failure was that the memory captured only some activities mentioned across the message span and omitted one that was explicitly stated in a later message, making the memory incomplete for retrieval. The rule to sweep every source message for all distinct durable items and include each one in the aggregated candidate applies to any multi-message event recap, where a future question may target any of those items.

payload.name: Preserve item-specific attributes in list extractions
payload.description: When a message lists multiple items with individual reasons, attributes, or qualifications, extract each item together with its attached attribute instead of recording only the item names.
content: During extraction, whenever a source message lists several items (recommendations, preferences, offers) and gives each item its own reason or attribute, capture each item with its attribute intact (e.g., 'item X is calming and cute') rather than bundling only the item names into one summary.
When updating an existing memory from such a list, merge the item-specific attribute details into the enriched content instead of replacing them with a name-only enumeration.

candidates.solves: When a message lists multiple items (recommendations, preferences, or offers) and attaches individual reasons or attributes to each, extraction often keeps only the item names and drops the per-item attributes. This causes later questions about a specific attribute to fail because the memory lacks the binding. The rule applies to any future session where a list with item-specific details needs to be remembered for attribute-based queries.

payload.name: preserve_all_enumerated_qualities
payload.description: When a user message explicitly lists multiple qualities, reasons, or attributes for a preference or judgment, preserve every listed item in the memory content and do not add unstated traits.
content: When a statement enumerates multiple qualities, reasons, or attributes (e.g., 'brave, selfless, down-to-earth'), capture the full list in the extracted memory content; do not reduce it to a subset or paraphrase with unstated attributes.

Before committing any preference or judgment memory, compare its attributes against the source message: every explicitly listed attribute must be present, and any attribute not in the source must be removed.

candidates.solves: Failures occur when users enumerate several qualities or reasons for a preference and the agent stores only a subset or adds an unstated trait, leaving later answers incomplete. Always preserve the full explicit enumeration and forbid unstated attributes, during both candidate extraction and ADD/UPDATE of preference memories. Applies to any preference or judgment statement that explicitly lists attributes, not when attributes are only implied.

payload.name: Preserve attributed qualities in opinion memories
payload.description: When extracting an opinion or evaluation, include any specific qualities or attributes the speaker states (taste, texture, appearance, etc.), not only the overall verdict.
content: During extraction, if a message contains someone's evaluation of an item and explicitly describes specific qualities (e.g., 'rich and creamy', 'spicy', 'soft'), preserve those attributes in the candidate memory content alongside the overall verdict, because later questions may target those attributes.
If multiple attributes are listed, include them concisely; do not drop details in favor of a generic summary.

candidates.solves: The failure: extraction kept only the overall judgment ('delicious') and dropped explicit attributes ('rich and creamy'), so later detail questions failed. The rule applies to any opinion/review extraction where the speaker states both a verdict and specific qualities, across topics such as food, products, or media. It is bounded to messages with explicit attributes; it does not require inventing details or keeping irrelevant verbosity.

payload.name: Preserve explicit evaluative claims in extraction
payload.description: When extracting memory candidates from a message with both descriptive details and explicit positive/negative assessments, promises, or recommendations, include the explicit evaluative claim in the candidate content.
content: During candidate extraction, if a speaker makes an explicit evaluative or attitudinal claim (e.g., a promise, warning, or recommendation), preserve that claim as part of the candidate content rather than only summarizing the descriptive context.

Before finalizing an ADD, verify that each distinct explicit claim in the source message is represented in a candidate; if one is missing, expand the candidate or create a separate memory anchored to the same source.

candidates.solves: During construction extraction, when a message contains both a descriptive summary and an explicit evaluative or attitudinal statement (such as a promise, recommendation, or prediction), the candidate should preserve that explicit claim instead of paraphrasing only the surrounding description. This applies to any future extraction where a distinct direct statement would otherwise be lost; it does not require storing every subjective phrase.

payload.name: Preserve specific claims and skip invented details in extraction
payload.description: When extracting a memory candidate from a message that states a specific plan, object, or preference, preserve the specific wording and do not add participants or conditions that are not mentioned in the evidence.
content: During extraction, if the source message names a specific object, phrase, or plan, keep that exact or near-exact wording in the memory content; do not replace it with a more general or abstract paraphrase.

Do not introduce people, entities, times, or conditions that are absent from the source message. If a participant is not stated in the evidence, do not assert their presence or involvement in the memory.
Before finalizing a candidate, check that every noun, participant, and qualifier in the candidate is present in or directly implied by the source message; otherwise remove the unsupported element.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates often drift from the source message by generalizing a specific phrase into a vaguer paraphrase and by adding plausible but unsupported details, such as naming a participant never mentioned. This applies when drafting a memory from a user statement of a plan, event, or preference; the extractor should preserve the concrete wording of key claims and include only entities and conditions present in the evidence. It does not apply to summarization of long multi-claim messages where compression is unavoidable, nor to CRUD operations on existing memories.

payload.name: Preserve enumerated recommendations in extraction
payload.description: When a message contains an explicit recommendation of multiple concrete items, supplies, or tools, extract each named item rather than summarizing the recommendation generically.
content: During extraction, if a speaker recommends or lists concrete items to acquire, create memory content that names each item, not just 'recommend supplies'.
If memory compaction is needed, keep the enumerated items or group them by category while retaining all named specifics.
Do not add inferred items absent from the message.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates sometimes compress an explicit list of recommended concrete items into a generic phrase such as 'recommend supplies,' losing details needed later. This skill applies when a speaker names specific items/tools to acquire; preserve each enumerated item in the candidate/memory instead of only noting that a recommendation was made. It does not apply to general offers without listed items or to non-enumerable abstractions.

payload.name: PreserveDistinctFactsPerSubject
payload.description: When extracting memories, if a message states multiple distinct facts about the same subject (e.g., preferences, reactions), preserve each as a separate candidate instead of summarizing them into one memory and losing a claim.
content: During candidate extraction, when a single message contains multiple distinct factual claims about the same subject, create a separate candidate for each claim rather than one merged summary that may drop a claim.

If the message includes a specific behavioral reaction or emotion (e.g., 'they were so confused', 'she hates rain') alongside a general preference, store both—the preference does not subsume the reaction.
After extraction, check that every key claim in the message appears in at least one candidate; if a fact is needed for recall, it must be represented in memory.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates sometimes merge several facts about one subject from a single message and drop a specific behavioral reaction, so later recall of that reaction fails. This rule applies whenever a future message about a person or pet contains both a broad preference and a distinct emotional/behavioral response; it instructs preserving each separable claim as its own candidate. It does not apply to judging memory sufficiency or to merging identical claims.

payload.name: PreserveAllListedDetailsInExtraction
payload.description: When a source message lists multiple distinct activities, traits, or uses compound phrases like 'X and Y', apply during extraction to keep every enumerated item in the memory content.
content: During candidate extraction, if the source lists several distinct details or uses a compound phrase ('A and B'), include every item in the memory content. Do not omit or merge any listed element for brevity; if needed, use a compact list format to retain all details.

candidates.solves: This addresses extraction-stage lossy summarization where a memory candidate drops items from an enumerated list or truncates a compound phrase (e.g., capturing only 'worries' from 'worries and hopes'). It applies to future construction sessions whenever a user message enumerates multiple facts about a subject, ensuring evidence-complete memories.

payload.name: Extract all distinct facts per message
payload.description: When a user message contains multiple independent durable facts (events, states, decisions), extract a separate candidate for each distinct fact instead of collapsing them into one memory.
content: During extraction, scan each message for every independently stated durable fact (e.g., an item breaking, a repair/sale decision, a trip, a purchase). Generate one candidate per distinct fact, even if the message also contains a more salient event.
Do not merge distinct facts from one message into a single memory when that would lose information; the CRUD stage can merge or deduplicate related memories later.
If a fact's durability is uncertain, include it as a candidate rather than dropping it; sufficiency checking and merge happen in the batched CRUD stage.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction often collapses a user message containing multiple independent durable facts into a single candidate that captures only the most salient fact, silently dropping explicit facts (e.g., an item breaking and a separate trip). This skill applies to any future message where one utterance states several distinct durable events, states, or decisions; it requires one candidate per explicit fact so later queries can retrieve each fact.

payload.name: PreserveCompleteEnumeratedInterests
payload.description: When a message lists multiple hobbies, interests, or activities, use this before extracting memory to ensure every listed item is preserved, and during CRUD to merge missing items into existing memories.
content: During extraction, when a message enumerates multiple hobbies, interests, or activities (e.g., items joined by 'and', commas, or bullets), create a candidate that includes every listed item; do not omit items that the speaker does not elaborate on.

During CRUD, before ADDing a partial candidate, check the retrieved memory pool for an existing profile covering the same subject and overlapping interests; if found, MERGE/UPDATE to add the newly listed items rather than creating a redundant partial memory.
Apply this to any list of interests, preferences, or activities; do not apply to statements about a single activity or to general statements that do not enumerate concrete items.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: a candidate extracted from a message listing several hobbies captured only the elaborated one, leaving another listed hobby absent from memory. Abstract mechanism: extraction should treat enumerations as complete sets; dropping any item creates coverage gaps. This applies to any future message where a user enumerates multiple interests, preferences, or activities, and to CRUD decisions that should merge the new items into existing per-person profiles.

payload.name: ExtractPerMessageNewFactsWithinSessions
payload.description: When a later user message in the same session adds distinct facts about an already-extracted activity, create an additional extraction candidate instead of skipping the message.
content: During candidate extraction, process each user message independently: if a message reveals any new memory-worthy fact about the user, generate a candidate even when an earlier message already produced a memory on the same overall topic.

Do not skip or merge a later message merely because it elaborates on an already-extracted activity; when it adds distinct sub-activities, attributes, or aspects, emit a separate candidate so the full set of facts is preserved.

candidates.solves: The extraction stage skipped a user message that added distinct activities (studying characters/themes, making recommendations) beyond an already-extracted activity, so those facts were never stored. The mechanism is under-extraction across messages that elaborate on a known topic; future conversations where a user expands an activity over multiple turns risk the same loss. The rule—emit a candidate for every message with new facts—applies generally; it does not apply when a later message only repeats or confirms existing memories.

payload.name: Extract Each Distinct Claim from Compound Statements
payload.description: When a message contains more than one distinct proposition (e.g., a stressor and a source of cheer), during extraction create a separate memory candidate for each rather than dropping one.
content: When a single message states multiple distinct facts (for example, a stressful situation and what brings the speaker joy or comfort), extract each fact as its own memory candidate; do not collapse them into one candidate that omits a claim.

Before finalizing an extracted candidate, re-read the message for any additional factual claims—such as a coping source, preference, or relationship—that were not captured, and add them as separate candidates.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: extraction captured only the stress clause and omitted the separate claim 'turtles cheer me up', so a supported fact was never stored. The abstract mechanism is failing to split a compound utterance into its distinct factual claims. The rule applies whenever one message contains multiple separable propositions (e.g., a negative event paired with a positive coping source), across any topic; it does not apply when a message contains only a single claim or when the unsupported fact is not present in the evidence.

payload.name: Preserve all explicitly enumerated message elements
payload.description: When extracting or updating memories from a message that explicitly lists multiple reasons, traits, interests, or items joined by connectors (and, plus, also), include every listed element in the candidate or memory content.
content: During candidate extraction, if a message explicitly enumerates multiple elements (e.g., 'passionate about X and Y'), include each enumerated element in the candidate content; do not selectively capture only a subset.

Before finalizing an ADD/UPDATE/MERGE, verify that no explicitly co-enumerated element from the source message is missing from the candidate or resulting memory; if one is missing, add the complete set.

candidates.solves: During candidate extraction, an explicitly multi-item list in a message (e.g., a person names several reasons or passions joined by 'and'/'plus') is sometimes partially captured, dropping one or more enumerated elements; later questions about the omitted item cannot be answered from memory. This rule requires preserving every explicitly co-enumerated element in extraction and verifying completeness during CRUD, and applies to any future message that lists multiple distinct items. It is not meant for summarizing implied or verbose background beyond enumerated facts.

payload.name: preserve-enumerated-items-in-extraction
payload.description: When extracting memories from a message that contains an explicit enumeration of experiences, preferences, reasons, or attributes, include every listed item and do not drop any element during summarization.
content: During extraction, when the source message explicitly enumerates items (comma-separated, or joined by 'and'/'or'), preserve every listed item in the candidate memory content. Avoid summary paraphrases that drop any enumerated element.
If all items cannot fit comfortably in one candidate, still capture the full list in the candidate; do not omit items for brevity.

candidates.solves: The failure occurred when an extraction candidate paraphrased a user's explicit three-item enumeration and dropped one item, creating memory that failed to cover the full claim. This rule applies to any future message that explicitly lists multiple distinct experiences, preferences, reasons, or attributes: each enumerated item must be preserved in the extracted memory. It does not apply to inferring unmentioned details or merging redundant phrasing.

payload.name: Preserve all enumerated advice in memory extraction
payload.description: When extracting a candidate memory or enriching an existing memory from a message that lists multiple distinct pieces of advice, requirements, or criteria, ensure every enumerated point is explicitly captured.
content: When extracting a memory candidate, parse the full source message for every distinct piece of advice or criterion; do not stop after the first one or two items.

If a message contains several separate points joined by 'and', commas, or list-like phrasing, include each point explicitly in the candidate content or enrichment update; dropping any later item is an extraction error.
When updating an existing memory with new advice, append all missing points rather than overwriting with a partial restatement, so no enumerated element is lost.

candidates.solves: Future problems where a source message gives several distinct pieces of advice or criteria and a memory candidate captures only a subset, usually dropping the last item, causing answers to miss claims. Applies during extraction and enrichment whenever a message explicitly enumerates multiple distinct points; not applicable when a message conveys one idea or when condensing paraphrases is intended.

payload.name: Preserve-all-stated-attributes-in-memory
payload.description: When a single message states multiple distinct attributes or facts about the same event or entity, preserve every stated attribute when extracting a memory candidate or updating an existing memory; do not drop details while summarizing.
content: During extraction and during CRUD updates, when a source message explicitly lists multiple distinct attributes or facts about the same event or entity (e.g., 'story was gripping and the actors were great'), include every listed attribute in the resulting memory content; do not collapse the memory to a single overall impression that omits any explicitly stated detail.

candidates.solves: Extraction collapsed a multi-attribute message ('gripping and the actors were great') into one impression, dropping the actors detail so later evidence was missing. The rule applies to any future construction step where a source lists several distinct facts about one subject: keep each explicit attribute in the candidate or update, preventing partial memories.

payload.name: Capture-all-enumerated-goals-in-extraction
payload.description: When a message lists multiple distinct goals, preferences, or plans in one utterance, ensure extraction captures each distinct item.
content: During candidate extraction, when a single message lists multiple distinct goals, preferences, plans, or intentions (e.g., joined by 'and', 'also', or commas), capture every distinct item—either as separate candidates or explicitly enumerated in one candidate—rather than keeping only the most salient item.
Before finalizing an extraction candidate for an enumerated list, re-read the source message to confirm each listed distinct item is represented.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is extraction dropping a distinct enumerated goal when a more salient one is stored. The reusable rule: when one utterance lists multiple distinct goals/preferences/plans, every item must be captured in extraction candidates. This applies to any future message enumerating separate user goals/preferences/plans; it does not apply when the listed items are paraphrases of a single goal.

payload.name: ExtractAllDistinctFactsFromListedMessage
payload.description: When a single message contains multiple distinct facts, events, or activities about the same subject, during extraction create separate candidates for each distinct fact, not only the most prominent item.
content: During candidate extraction, if one message enumerates multiple distinct facts, activities, or states about the same subject, create a separate compact memory candidate for each distinct fact instead of collapsing them into one candidate that captures only the most salient item.

When a later notable event shares a message with other ongoing activities, do not drop those activities; give each its own candidate with an appropriate world_start, or explicitly evaluate and justify why a particular fact is not durable.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that candidate extraction from a multi-fact message captured only the most salient event (a conference presentation) and dropped other enumerated activities (workshops), leaving a claim missing from memory. The rule to create a separate candidate for every distinct fact is a valid abstraction of salience-based omission and applies to any message that lists multiple facts, events, or activities about one subject, preventing incomplete memories and later recall failures.

payload.name: Preserve limiting qualifiers in extracted memories
payload.description: When extracting a memory candidate from a statement with quantifiers or qualifiers like 'a few', 'bits', 'some', 'partial', or 'almost', preserve them instead of generalizing to a whole or completed item.
content: During extraction, keep any quantifier or qualifier that materially limits or specifies the claim (e.g., 'a few bits', 'some pages', 'almost finished', 'partial draft'). Do not upgrade it to a full, complete, or whole version. If the source describes a portion or unfinished artifact, reflect that exact scope in the candidate content.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause was extraction normalizing 'a few bits for a screenplay' into 'a screenplay', dropping the quantifier 'bits' and inflating a partial work into a completed whole. This rule preserves limiting qualifiers and quantifiers during candidate extraction so that memories stay faithful to the source. It applies to any future statement containing modifiers such as 'a few', 'bits', 'some', 'partial', or 'almost' where dropping them would change the meaning, in any domain.

payload.name: Extract separate candidates for each distinct durable fact
payload.description: When a message states multiple distinct durable facts (e.g., how a skill was learned and who supported it), generate one memory candidate per fact instead of a single summary that omits some facts.
content: During candidate extraction, treat each distinct claim in a message as a separate durable fact (skills, preferences, events, relationships) and generate one candidate per claim; do not let a single summary drop any claim.

When a sentence contains multiple clauses with different predicates (e.g., 'I taught myself' and 'my dad was supportive'), create a separate candidate for each clause rather than only the clause that seems to fit an existing memory narrative.
If a fact is stated in an earlier message, extract it from that message; a later restatement is not a substitute for capturing the original occurrence.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that the extraction stage produced no candidate for the clearly stated fact 'learned to play on my own', and a later candidate captured only parental support while dropping the self-teaching claim. The reusable failure mechanism is treating a multi-fact message as one summary instead of several independent durable facts. This rule applies to any future utterance containing multiple facts about skills, preferences, events, or relationships, ensuring no durable claim is lost when another claim in the same message is captured.

payload.name: Preserve all enumerated items in extraction
payload.description: Use when a source message lists two or more distinct items (reasons, qualities, observations, preferences) and the construction extraction candidate must capture all of them.
content: During extraction, when the evidence explicitly enumerates multiple distinct items in a list (e.g., 'growth, improvement, and confidence'), include every listed item in the candidate content; do not replace the list with a single broader or synonymous term that drops any element.

If the candidate paraphrases but would omit one of the enumerated items, rephrase to name each item explicitly, even if the memory must be slightly longer, so that future questions about any single item remain answerable.

candidates.solves: When a source message explicitly enumerates multiple distinct items as a set (e.g., reasons, qualities, observations, preferences), the extraction candidate must preserve each enumerated element rather than paraphrase the whole list into a single broader term that omits any item. Future questions may test any one listed item, so losing a facet at extraction makes that fact unrecoverable later. This applies to any extraction candidate where the raw evidence contains a clear list of two or more discrete elements.

payload.name: Preserve enumerated facts and avoid unsupported objects
payload.description: When a user message explicitly lists multiple purposes, attributes, or uses of an entity, apply during candidate extraction and memory updates to capture every listed item without omitting any and without adding objects absent from the source.
content: During candidate extraction, if the source message explicitly enumerates multiple facts, purposes, or attributes of an entity, include all enumerated items in the candidate content; do not drop any listed item.
Do not introduce objects, tools, or unstated details into memory content unless they appear explicitly in the source message; paraphrase only what is actually said.
During UPDATE or MERGE, preserve every explicitly stated detail from the new source; if replacing a memory, carry the full set of stated facts forward rather than a partial subset.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is extraction that omitted two explicitly stated purposes and inserted an unmentioned whiteboard. The abstract failure mechanism is unfaithful paraphrase of enumerated source facts, leading to incomplete and hallucinated memory content. This skill applies to future construction tasks where a user lists multiple attributes, uses, or goals of an entity; it does not apply when the source is vague, when facts are implicit, or when a legitimate summary intentionally condenses repeated information.

payload.name: Preserve all distinct claims when extracting preferences
payload.description: Use during extraction when a single message states multiple distinct preferences, values, or evaluations about different activities, objects, or people; ensure each claim is captured before finalizing memory candidates.
content: When a source message contains multiple distinct preferences, values, or evaluations about different activities, objects, or people, generate one candidate per distinct claim, or one candidate that explicitly preserves every claim in wording.

Before finalizing extraction for a message, check that each distinct claim in the message appears in at least one candidate; do not drop a claim just because another claim in the same message seems more salient.
During batched ADD/UPDATE/MERGE, do not let a new candidate overwrite or merge away an existing memory claim that is still true; preserve all distinct true claims from the source.

candidates.solves: A single source message often lists several independent preferences or evaluations (e.g., time with one activity is valuable, time with another is relaxing). The diagnosed failure was that extraction kept only the more salient claim, so the stored memory missed a required fact. The skill ensures every distinct claim in a multi-claim utterance is preserved during extraction and not dropped during updates/merges. It applies to future messages containing parallel, contrastive, or enumerated statements about a person's preferences.

payload.name: Faithful extraction of enumerated claims
payload.description: When extracting memory candidates from a message that lists multiple distinct claims, strategies, or reasons, preserve each explicitly stated item and do not add details absent from the source.
content: During extraction, paraphrase the utterance completely: every explicitly stated claim (e.g., each strategy, reason, or preference the speaker lists) must appear in the candidate content; do not drop any item.

Do not add details not present in the source text, such as invented activities or examples. If a detail is not in the message, exclude it. Prefer omitting unstated embellishments over risking hallucination, but never omit stated claims.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: extraction dropped Gina's explicitly stated 'reminding myself of my successes and progress' and added an unsupported 'dancing' detail, corrupting grounding. Abstract mechanism: candidate extraction can silently substitute or omit stated items when summarizing a multi-part utterance. The rule forces faithful, complete extraction of explicit claims without invented details. Applies to any future extraction where a speaker enumerates strategies, reasons, preferences, or facts.

payload.name: ExtractEachDurableFactSeparately
payload.description: When a single message contains more than one distinct durable fact (e.g., an action plus a background business/job/ownership state), create a separate extraction candidate for each fact during construction extraction.
content: During candidate extraction, treat each distinct durable fact in a message as its own candidate instead of merging them into the most salient action.

If a message mentions both an ongoing/enacted event (e.g., launching an ad campaign) and a durable status that explains it (e.g., starting/owning the store), emit one candidate for the event and one for the status fact.
Before finalizing a candidate list, check each message for background facts that future questions could compare across people; do not let a concrete action candidate absorb them.

candidates.solves: Extraction collapsed multiple distinct durable facts in one message into a single action-centric candidate, dropping a background fact (e.g., starting one's own business) that later cross-person comparisons need. This rule forces a separate candidate for each independently verifiable durable fact, preserving both foreground events and background states. Applies to any message combining an activity with an underlying status or ownership fact.

payload.name: Preserve all enumerated reasons in memory extraction
payload.description: When a message lists several distinct reasons, traits, or attributes about a subject, apply this during extraction and CRUD to ensure every enumerated item is stored and none is dropped.
content: When a message explicitly lists multiple distinct reasons, traits, or attributes (e.g., 'because of A and B', 'it is X and Y'), include each enumerated item as a separate clause in the extraction candidate; do not collapse them into one general phrase.

During CRUD, when enriching an existing memory, compare the source message against the proposed content and add any enumerated reason/attribute that is missing, even if the memory already covers part of the list.
Before finalizing a candidate or update, re-check the source message to confirm that every explicitly stated fact is represented; if any is absent, expand the candidate content.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates sometimes drop one of several explicit reasons or attributes when a speaker lists multiple traits or justifications in one message, leaving memory incomplete for later questions. A rule that every enumerated fact must be carried into the candidate (and into enrichments during CRUD) directly addresses this mechanism and applies to any future message that lists multiple preferences, causes, features, or conditions.

payload.name: Preserve exact evaluative wording during extraction
payload.description: When extracting memory candidates from a message, if the source explicitly states an evaluative description, preserve that exact wording instead of replacing it with a synonym or paraphrase.
content: During extraction, when a source message contains an explicit evaluation or description, keep the speaker's exact adjective or phrase in the candidate content; do not substitute a near-synonym.
Before accepting a candidate that describes a subjective experience or quality, check the source message and confirm every distinctive evaluative word appears verbatim in the candidate.
Use generic summary language only when the source itself does not state a specific evaluative word; never normalize strong explicit wording into a weaker paraphrase.

candidates.solves: Caused by extraction paraphrasing an explicit evaluative adjective into a near-synonym, persisting in memory and failing exact-description recall. The reusable rule is to preserve exact evaluative wording when extracting memories from source statements. Applies to future extractions of explicit subjective descriptions; not applicable when source lacks exact wording or a neutral summary is intended.

payload.name: Preserve enumerated facts and do not skip unbacked candidates
payload.description: When extracting a candidate from a message that lists multiple distinct items, or when deciding whether to SKIP a candidate as duplicate, preserve every listed item and only SKIP if an existing memory covers it.
content: During extraction, when the source message enumerates multiple distinct items (e.g., 'chatted about X and Y', 'likes A, B, and C'), include each item explicitly in the candidate; do not replace the list with a broader paraphrase that omits any listed item.

During CRUD, before marking a candidate as SKIP because it is 'duplicate or already fully represented', check that there is an existing memory that actually covers the candidate's claims. If no such memory exists, ADD or MERGE the candidate instead of skipping it.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates that paraphrase a message containing multiple enumerated facts often drop one item, and the missing fact is later judged absent; candidates are also wrongly SKIPped as duplicates when no existing memory supports them. Applies to any construction session where one utterance lists distinct facts; does not require verbatim message reproduction, only preservation of every listed fact and evidence-backed duplicate checks.

payload.name: ExtractAllFactsFromMultiFactMessages
payload.description: When a user message states multiple distinct facts about the same subject and an extraction candidate is created, use separate candidates or full coverage so that no explicit fact is dropped.
content: During candidate extraction, a message containing multiple distinct facts must be covered by the candidate set as a whole; do not let one thematic candidate omit other explicit facts from the same message.
When facts in one message do not share a coherent theme, split them into separate ADD/UPDATE candidates instead of merging them under the dominant topic.
Before committing a batch, verify each source message against the candidates/updates it produced; any explicit fact missing from all of them must be added.

candidates.solves: An extraction candidate built around one dominant theme dropped an explicit fact from the same multi-fact message, and no later update restored it. The rule: treat each source message as fully covered by its candidate set—split distinct facts into separate candidates or ensure the combined set includes every explicit fact. Applies to any extraction batch where a message contributes several facts; not to choosing which facts are worth retaining.

payload.name: Update completed ongoing events with duration
payload.description: When new evidence completes an ongoing event already stored in memory, update that existing event memory with end time or duration before adding a new completion event.
content: During extraction and CRUD decisions, if a message states that an already-memorized ongoing event (same subject and activity) has finished, prefer UPDATE or MERGE the existing event memory to set world_end and record the duration.
Do not ADD a separate completion event unless it conveys new facts distinct from the existing event.
When the start date is known and the end is expressed relatively (e.g., 'last month'), resolve the end date from the message timestamp and compute the duration in the updated memory.

candidates.solves: When later messages reveal the end of an already-stored ongoing event, the agent often adds a separate completion event and never records the duration, so future questions about how long the event lasted cannot be answered. This rule forces updating the existing event memory with its end time or duration, consolidating temporal facts in one memory. It applies whenever a stored ongoing event is later completed; it does not apply to unrelated new events.

payload.name: Preserve time details when extracting event memories
payload.description: When a message describes an event, possession, or state and also states when it happened (explicit date or relative phrase such as 'a few years ago'), apply during extraction to keep that temporal detail in the memory instead of omitting it.
content: During extraction of an event, possession, or state, if the source message states when it happened (explicit date or relative phrase like 'a few years ago', 'last month'), include that temporal detail in the memory content and/or set an accurate time field; do not omit it while summarizing meaning, symbolism, or other attributes.
Resolve relative time phrases from the message/session timestamp to compute the event time; if precision is uncertain, preserve the original phrase so the fact remains answerable.

candidates.solves: Extraction dropped an explicit relative time ('a few years ago') while summarizing a tattoo's meaning, so the event memory couldn't answer 'when'.
